n-m-h2-explog-07.material: Eunseo wants to find log_6 12 without a calculator. If she is told just one of the values below, she wants to check whether she can express log_6 12 in terms of that value using only the properties of logarithms and the four arithmetic operations. (log_6 12 is the logarithm of 12 with base 6.)
n-m-h2-explog-07.thinking.1: Reducing to the same value by changing the base
n-m-h2-explog-07.prereq.2: The relationship between reciprocals and logarithms
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.prompt: Select all values such that knowing just that one value lets you express log_6 12 in terms of it using only the properties of logarithms and the four arithmetic operations.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.hint.0: Try changing the base of log_6 12 to 2 or 3, or writing 12 and 6 as products of 2 and 3, to see which single logarithm can express it.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether each choice carries the same information as that one logarithm (whether it can be converted into it by a formula).
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.a: With log_10 2 alone, you cannot know log_10 3, so you cannot express both 12 and 6.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.b: You missed the information that converts to a single logarithm, as in log_2 6=1+log_2 3.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.c: You missed that using log_6 3=1−log_6 2 lets you express log_6 12.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.d: It is unrelated to 2 and 3, so it does not help.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.e: You missed that log_3 2 is the reciprocal of log_2 3.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.r.f: You missed that changing log_6 12 to base 2 leaves only log_2 3.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s1.explain: log_6 12=log_2 12/log_2 6=(2+log_2 3)/(1+log_2 3), so p=log_2 3 alone is enough. log_2 6=1+p, log_3 2=1/p, and log_6 2=1/(1+p) can also be converted to and from p. log_10 2 does not work unless you know log_10 3, and log_5 7 has no relation to 2 and 3.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.prompt: Let p=log_2 3. Express log_6 12 in terms of p.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.hint.0: Change the base to 2 and write the numerator and denominator each as values of log_2.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write log_2 12 and log_2 6 as products of 2 and 3, and use the properties of logarithms to express them in terms of p.
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you find log_2 12=2+log_2 3 and log_2 6=1+log_2 3?
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: In your expression with p, did you put the numerator and denominator the right way up?
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you substitute p=1.585 and check that log_6 12≈1.387?
n-m-h2-explog-07.s.s2.model.1: Changing the base to 2 gives log_2 12 / log_2 6 = (2+p)/(1+p).

n-m-h2-explog-08.title: Checking a solution that counted digits using common logarithms
n-m-h2-explog-08.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that uses common logarithms to find the number of digits, and check how the number of digits changes at boundary values.
n-m-h2-explog-08.material: Seoyeon used common logarithms to find how many digits 3^50 has. (log 3=0.4771, and 3^50 is 3 to the 50th power.)
n-m-h2-explog-08.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in the solution
n-m-h2-explog-08.prereq.0: The meaning of the common logarithm
n-m-h2-explog-08.prereq.1: Powers of 10 and the number of digits
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Seoyeon's solution.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.hint.0: Check with a smaller number. How many digits does 10^2=100 have?
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that result side by side with the integer part of the logarithm, and see whether Seoyeon's 4th conclusion is right.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.line.0: To find the number of digits of 3^50, take the common logarithm of both sides.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.line.3: Since 10^23≤3^50<10^24, the integer part 23 is the number of digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the first one that goes wrong. 10^23 is a 1 followed by 23 zeros, which has 24 digits. So an N with 10^23≤N<10^24 has 24 digits, and you must add 1 to the integer part 23 to get the number of digits. Line 5 is the result that follows from line 4.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.prompt: Write the correct number of digits of 3^50, and write which of Seoyeon's judgments needs to be corrected and how.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of digits of 10^1, 10^2, 10^3 and find the difference between the exponent and the number of digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.hint.1: Apply the pattern you found to the N with log N=23.855.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that 10^2=100 has 3 digits?
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 1 must be added to the integer part?
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say how many digits N has if N is at least 10^23 and less than 10^24?
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.model.0: Since log 3^50=23.855, 10^23≤3^50<10^24. 10^23 has 24 digits, so 3^50 has 24 digits. You must add 1 to the integer part 23.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.model.1: 10 to the 23rd power has 24 digits, so 3^50 also has 24 digits. Seoyeon wrote the integer part directly as the number of digits, but she should have added 1.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s2.model.2: The integer part is 23, and the number of digits is 23+1=24.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.prompt: Among the positive numbers N whose common logarithms are given below, select all that have 8 digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write each N as a range between powers of 10. For example, if log N=7.2, between which two powers is it?
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.hint.1: When the logarithm is an integer, write exactly which power of 10 N is, and count the digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.r.a: You knew that when the logarithm is an integer, N=10^7, which has 8 digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.r.b: N=10^8 has 9 digits. If the integer part is 8, the number of digits is 9.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.r.c: This is the judgment of adding 1 to the integer part 7 to get 8 digits.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.r.d: 6.99 has integer part 6, so it has 7 digits. Being close to 7 is different from being at least 7.
n-m-h2-explog-08.s.s3.explain: If the integer part of log N is n, then N has n+1 digits. If log N=7.0, then N=10^7, which has 8 digits, and if it is 7.2, then 10^7≤N<10^8, so it has 8 digits. 6.99 gives 7 digits and 8.0 gives 9 digits.

n-m-h2-explog-09.title: Judging symmetry between graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions
n-m-h2-explog-09.goal: Check symmetry claims between several graphs using formulas to decide which are true and false, and show the reason for one claim with a single formula.
n-m-h2-explog-09.material: Seungwoo summarized the symmetry relationships among the graphs of the exponential and logarithmic functions with bases 2 and 1/2. The logarithm with base 1/2 is written log_{1/2}x.
n-m-h2-explog-09.thinking.1: Turning relationships between graphs into formulas
n-m-h2-explog-09.thinking.2: Finding the correct symmetry for a wrong claim
n-m-h2-explog-09.prereq.0: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions
n-m-h2-explog-09.prereq.1: Inverse functions and symmetry about the line y=x
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.prompt: Select all the correct statements among those Seungwoo summarized.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.hint.0: For each pair of graphs, pick one point and find its coordinates, then check how that point would have to be moved to land on the other graph.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.hint.1: First write down how symmetry about the y-axis and symmetry about the line y=x each change the coordinates of a point.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.o.a: The graphs of y=2^x and y=(1/2)^x are symmetric about the y-axis
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.r.a: Since (1/2)^x=2^(−x), it is the graph with the sign of x changed. You missed a correct statement.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.o.b: The graphs of y=log_2 x and y=log_{1/2} x are symmetric about the y-axis
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.r.b: Log functions are defined only for x>0, so they cannot be symmetric about the y-axis.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.o.c: The graphs of y=2^x and y=log_2 x are symmetric about the line y=x
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.r.c: They are inverse functions of each other, so they are symmetric about y=x. You missed a correct statement.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.o.d: The graphs of y=2^x and y=log_{1/2} x are symmetric about the line y=x
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.r.d: The inverse function of 2^x is log_2 x, not log_{1/2} x.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s1.explain: Since (1/2)^x=2^(−x), y=2^x and y=(1/2)^x are symmetric about the y-axis. y=2^x and y=log_2 x are inverse functions of each other, so they are symmetric about y=x. log_{1/2} x has domain x>0, so it cannot be symmetric about the y-axis, and it is not the inverse function of 2^x either.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.prompt: Write the line about which the graphs of y=log_2 x and y=log_{1/2} x are symmetric, and show the reason with a formula.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.hint.0: Rewrite log_{1/2} x as a logarithm with base 2. Compare the y-values of the two formulas at the same x.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.hint.1: Look at how the y-values are related, and say along which axis direction that relationship moves a point.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you get log_{1/2} x=−log_2 x by changing the base?
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Using point coordinates, did you say that at the same x the two y-values differ only in sign?
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say how symmetry about the x-axis moves a point?
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.model.0: log_{1/2} x=log_2 x / log_2(1/2)=−log_2 x. At the same x the y-values differ only in sign, so the graphs are symmetric about the x-axis.
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.model.1: It is symmetric about the x-axis. Changing the base turns log_{1/2} x into −log_2 x, so it is the graph where the point (x, y) has been moved to (x, −y).
n-m-h2-explog-09.s.s2.model.2: They are symmetric about the x-axis. y=log_{1/2} x is the same as y=−log_2 x, so the y-values of the two graphs have opposite signs.

n-m-h2-explog-10.title: Finding positive pairs for which log(a+b)=log a+log b holds
n-m-h2-explog-10.goal: Check by building examples yourself whether the general fact "the logarithm of a sum is not the sum of the logarithms" has exceptions, and organize the condition as a formula.
n-m-h2-explog-10.material: log(a+b)=log a+log b is an equation that usually does not hold. But among positive numbers a and b, is there a pair for which it holds? (log is the common logarithm.)
n-m-h2-explog-10.thinking.0: Making examples where it holds yourself
n-m-h2-explog-10.thinking.1: Turning a sum of logarithms into a logarithm of a product
n-m-h2-explog-10.thinking.2: Finding the common condition of the examples
n-m-h2-explog-10.prereq.0: The property of logarithms log a+log b=log ab
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.prompt: Enter three different pairs of positive numbers a, b for which log(a+b)=log a+log b holds. (A pair with a and b swapped counts as the same pair. Decimals are fine.)
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.hint.0: Combine the sum of logarithms on the right into a single logarithm and compare it with the left side.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write what the arguments must be if the two logarithms are equal, then choose a and find b.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.ok.c1: a and b are both positive.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.fail.c1: a and b must both be positive.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.ok.c2: a+b and ab are equal, so log(a+b)=log a+log b holds.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.fail.c2: a+b and ab are different, so the two logarithms are not equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.explain: Since log a+log b=log ab, the equation holds when log(a+b)=log ab, that is, when a+b=ab. (2, 2), (3, 1.5), and (5, 1.25) all work. We used the fact that two logarithms are equal only if their arguments are equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.prompt: Write as a formula the relationship between a and b that holds in the pairs you found, and write why that relationship makes the two expressions equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.hint.0: For each pair you found, calculate a+b and ab and write them side by side.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.hint.1: Combine log a+log b into a single logarithm and write what the argument is.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write log a+log b=log ab?
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that if the logarithms are equal, the arguments are equal?
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.model.0: Since log a+log b=log ab, for log(a+b)=log ab we need a+b=ab. This is because if two logarithms are equal, their arguments are equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.model.1: The sum and the product of a and b must be equal (ab=a+b). This is because a sum of logarithms equals the logarithm of the product of the arguments, and if logarithms are equal, their arguments are equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s1.because.model.2: It is enough that (a−1)(b−1)=1. Expanding gives ab−a−b+1=1, so ab=a+b, and log a+log b=log ab=log(a+b).
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose the correct statement about positive numbers a, b for which log(a+b)=log a+log b holds.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.hint.0: If a is at most 1, take b to be positive and compare which of ab and a+b is greater.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.hint.1: Among the pairs satisfying a+b=ab, compare the sizes of a and b with each other.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.o.a: One of a and b can be less than 1
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.r.a: If a≤1, then ab≤b<a+b, so a+b cannot equal ab.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.o.b: a and b are both greater than 1
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.r.b: You knew that if a≤1 or b≤1, the product becomes smaller than the sum, so they cannot be equal.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.o.c: a and b are both less than 1
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.r.c: If both are less than 1, the product is much smaller than the sum.
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.o.d: One of a and b must be 2
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.r.d: There are pairs without a 2, such as (3, 1.5).
n-m-h2-explog-10.s.s2.explain: If a≤1, then ab≤b<a+b, so a+b cannot equal ab. The same holds when b≤1. So in the pairs that work, a and b are both greater than 1. Since (a−1)(b−1)=1, when one gets closer to 1, the other gets larger.

n-m-h2-integ-01.title: Are the value of a definite integral and the area under a graph the same thing?
n-m-h2-integ-01.topic: Definite integrals and area: signed area
n-m-h2-integ-01.goal: Understand that a definite integral is "signed area," counting the part below the x-axis as negative, build a case where the definite integral is 0 but the area is not 0, and explain the reason and how to find the area.
n-m-h2-integ-01.material: There is the graph of f(x)=x²−2x, the x-axis, and the interval 0≤x≤3. Hajun said, "∫₀³ f(x)dx=0, so the area between the graph and the x-axis is also 0," and Seoa said, "I don't think the area is 0." (∫₀³ is the definite integral from 0 to 3.)
n-m-h2-integ-01.thinking.0: Testing a claim with a specific function
n-m-h2-integ-01.thinking.1: Splitting the graph into the parts above and below the x-axis
n-m-h2-integ-01.thinking.2: Distinguishing the value of a definite integral from area
n-m-h2-integ-01.prereq.0: Calculating definite integrals of polynomial functions
n-m-h2-integ-01.prereq.1: The position of a function's graph relative to the x-axis
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct judgment about the area between the graph and the x-axis on this interval.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.hint.0: Sketch the graph of f(x)=x²−2x and mark where it is above the x-axis and where it is below within the interval.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis, split the interval at those points, calculate the definite integral on each piece separately, and compare the signs.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.o.a: The area is 0: because the value of the definite integral is the area between the graph and the x-axis
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.r.a: You treated the value of the definite integral and the area as the same thing. The part below the x-axis is counted as negative in a definite integral.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.o.b: The area is 0: because the graph meets the x-axis at a point within the interval
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.r.b: A point where the graph meets the x-axis is just a point and does not make the area 0. The shapes on both sides of that point have area.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.o.c: The area is not 0: because the upper part and the lower part have values with different signs and cancel
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.r.c: You thought about how positive and negative values can cancel inside a definite integral.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell: because the value of the definite integral alone tells nothing about the shape of the graph
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.r.d: Here f(x) is given, so we can check the shape of the graph directly.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s1.explain: f(x)=x²−2x=x(x−2) is below the x-axis on 0≤x≤2, so ∫₀² f=−4/3, and it is above on 2≤x≤3, so ∫₂³ f=4/3. They add to 0, but the area is 4/3+4/3=8/3. A definite integral is "signed area," counting the part below the x-axis as negative.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.prompt: For f(x)=x(x−a), enter two different pairs of positive integers (a, b) such that the definite integral ∫₀ᵇ f(x)dx=0. (1≤a≤20, 1≤b≤20)
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.hint.0: Expand ∫₀ᵇ x(x−a)dx and write it as an expression in a and b.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.hint.1: Work out what relationship between a and b makes that expression 0.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are positive integers within the range.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 1 to 20.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The value of ∫₀ᵇ x(x−a)dx is not 0. Expand and calculate b³/3−ab²/2.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s2.explain: ∫₀ᵇ x(x−a)dx=b³/3−ab²/2=b²(2b−3a)/6, so it is 0 when 2b=3a. Then b=1.5a is greater than a, so the interval [0,b] contains both a part below the x-axis (0<x<a) and a part above it (a<x<b). So even though the definite integral is 0, the area is not 0.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.prompt: Pick one of the pairs you just made and explain why the definite integral is 0 but the area is not, and how to find the area on that interval.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.hint.0: Using one of the pairs you made earlier, calculate the definite integrals of the part below the x-axis and the part above it separately and look at the signs.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.hint.1: Recall that area, like length, cannot be negative, and think about how the part below should be handled.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The definite integral ... because the part ... , and the area ...
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say how the part below the x-axis is counted inside the definite integral?
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that since area cannot be negative, you split the interval where the sign changes?
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.model.0: The definite integral of the part below the x-axis is negative and that of the part above is positive, so when added they cancel and give 0. For area, the part below must also be counted as positive, so split the interval at the point where the graph meets the x-axis, find each value, and add their absolute values.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.model.1: A definite integral is signed area, so the upper value and the lower value (negative) add up to 0. The actual area counts both as positive, so find them separately by splitting into [0,a] and [a,b], then add them.
n-m-h2-integ-01.s.s3.model.2: If you split the interval in two at the point where the graph meets the x-axis, one definite integral is positive and the other is negative. Even when their sum is 0, the area is |negative part|+|positive part|, which is greater than 0.

n-m-h2-integ-02.title: Checking Jimin's solution for a derivative given as a product
n-m-h2-integ-02.topic: Indefinite integrals: integrating a product and the constant of integration
n-m-h2-integ-02.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that recovered the original function from a derivative given as a product, and correct it properly by checking that differentiating the result brings you back.
n-m-h2-integ-02.material: This is Jimin's solution for finding the value of f(1) when f'(x)=(x+1)(x+2) and f(0)=2. (f' is read "f prime," and C is the constant of integration.)
n-m-h2-integ-02.thinking.0: Checking whether each line is the same expression as the line before
n-m-h2-integ-02.thinking.1: Testing a rule on a simple expression
n-m-h2-integ-02.prereq.1: Determining the constant of integration from an initial condition
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Jimin's solution.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s1.hint.0: Test whether the expression before and after each change is really the same by using the same method on a very simple expression.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether differentiating each line's result with respect to x gives back the integrand of the line just before it.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first one that is wrong. The indefinite integral of a product is not equal to the product of the separate indefinite integrals. For example, ∫x·x dx=x³/3, but ∫x dx × ∫x dx=x⁴/4. When it is a product, you must expand first. Since (x+1)(x+2)=x²+3x+2, f(x)=x³/3+3x²/2+2x+C, f(0)=2 gives C=2, and f(1)=1/3+3/2+2+2=35/6.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.prompt: After finishing the solution, what is the most direct check for catching an error like this yourself?
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether each check can catch a wrong solution, and pick out any check that always comes out right even for a wrong solution.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.hint.1: Recall the relationship between indefinite integrals and differentiation.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.o.a: Plug f(0)=2 into the f(x) you found and check that you really get 2
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.r.a: Since the constant of integration C was determined by this condition, it always comes out right. This check does not catch the error in integrating a product.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.o.b: Differentiate the f(x) you found with respect to x and check that f'(x)=(x+1)(x+2)
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.r.b: This check uses the fact that differentiating the result of an integral must give back the original expression.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.o.c: Check that the constant of integration C is attached to the result and not left out
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.r.c: C was attached. The problem with this solution is not the constant but the way of integrating.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.o.d: Calculate the value of f(1) once more with a calculator and check that you get the same value
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.r.d: Calculating the same expression again just gives the same value; it does not check whether the expression itself is right.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s2.explain: If you differentiate the f(x)=(x²/2+x)(x²/2+2x)+C you found, you do not get (x+1)(x+2), because of the product rule of differentiation. Checking whether differentiating brings you back to the original derivative is the most direct way to check an indefinite integral.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.prompt: Find the value of f(1) by a correct solution, and show with one simple expression that Jimin's second line does not hold.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.hint.0: If it is hard to integrate the product as it is, think about what form to change the product into so that you can integrate term by term.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.hint.1: Use Jimin's method on a very simple product such as x×x and compare it with the correct integral.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., First, if you ..., then f(1)=... . For example, ...
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In a simple expression (for example x×x), did you show with formulas that the two calculations give different results?
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: After finding the answer, did you check that differentiating brings you back to the derivative?
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.model.0: Expand (x+1)(x+2) into x²+3x+2 and integrate to get f(x)=x³/3+3x²/2+2x+C. Since f(0)=2, C=2, so f(1)=35/6. For example, ∫x·x dx is x³/3, but ∫x dx × ∫x dx is x⁴/4, so the integral of a product is not equal to the product of the integrals.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.model.1: f(1)=35/6. You must expand the product first and integrate term by term. The reason you must not multiply the separate integrals is that for x and x, one side gives x³/3 and the other x⁴/4, which are different.
n-m-h2-integ-02.s.s3.model.2: Expanding and integrating x²+3x+2 gives x³/3+(3/2)x²+2x+C. Since C=2, f(1)=35/6. Replacing the integral of a product with the product of integrals changes the degree already, so it is wrong (e.g., x·x).

n-m-h2-integ-03.title: If it came back to where it started, did it not move?
n-m-h2-integ-03.topic: Velocity and distance: change in position and distance traveled
n-m-h2-integ-03.goal: Understand, by revising your judgment each time information is revealed, that the definite integral of velocity is the change in position and differs from the distance traveled, and explain how to find the distance.
n-m-h2-integ-03.material: Information about a point P moving on a number line is revealed one piece at a time. The change in position is the integral of the velocity, and the distance traveled is the total of all the lengths actually covered.
n-m-h2-integ-03.thinking.0: Revising your judgment each time new information appears
n-m-h2-integ-03.thinking.1: Distinguishing change in position from distance traveled
n-m-h2-integ-03.thinking.2: Splitting the interval where the sign of the velocity changes
n-m-h2-integ-03.prereq.0: The relationship between velocity and position (change in position = definite integral of velocity)
n-m-h2-integ-03.prereq.1: Examining the sign of a quadratic function
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose a judgment using only the information revealed.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, think about whether "change in position" and "length covered" mean the same thing.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the motion of the point differs where the sign of the velocity changes.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.info: We found the change in position of point P, which started at t=0, up to t=6, and it was 0. That is, at t=6, P is at the place where it started.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this information alone, can we say that the distance P traveled is 0?
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The change in position is a value with direction (it has a sign), so it can be 0 even when the point goes out and comes back.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We can say so: the position is the same, so the distance traveled is also 0
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You treated change in position and distance traveled as the same thing. Even if it goes and comes back, the change is 0.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We cannot say so: if it went and came back, the distance is not 0 even though the change is 0
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You thought about how a change of 0 does not only mean "did not move."
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can say so: if the definite integral is 0, the velocity must always be 0
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even if the definite integral is 0, there can be intervals where the velocity is positive mixed with intervals where it is negative.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.info: The velocity turned out to be v(t)=t²−4t (0≤t≤6).
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: At what time does P change its direction of motion?
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.after: While the velocity is negative it moves in one direction, and while it is positive it moves in the opposite direction. The direction changes at t=4, where the sign changes.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: t=2: the graph of v(t) is lowest there, so the direction changes
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The place where v(t) has its minimum is where the speed is greatest, not where the direction changes.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: t=4: v(t)=0 and the sign changes on either side of it
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You checked that for v(t)=t(t−4), it is negative for 0<t<4 and positive for t>4.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It does not change direction: the moment the velocity is 0 is not a change of direction
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If the velocity is 0 and the sign changes, the direction changes.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.info: We found the change in position for each interval: −32/3 from 0 to 4, and +32/3 from 4 to 6.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the distance P actually traveled from t=0 to 6?
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The distance traveled is found by splitting the interval where the sign of the velocity changes and adding the magnitudes (absolute values) of the change in each interval. That is, ∫₀⁶|v(t)|dt=64/3.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 0: the sum of the two changes
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: When you add them, two movements in opposite directions cancel. This is the change in position.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 32/3: the magnitude of one of the two changes
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The interval of coming back is also part of the length actually covered.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 64/3: the sum of the magnitudes of the two changes
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You added all the lengths covered, regardless of direction.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked as if the distance would be 0 since P returned to the starting point, but when we looked at the sign of the velocity, there was an interval going out and an interval coming back. The change in position has a sign and cancels, but the distance traveled does not cancel.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.prompt: Write why the distance traveled is not 0 even though P is at the starting place at t=6, and explain how to find the distance traveled.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.hint.0: Put together the fact that P is at the starting point at t=6 and the signs of the velocity before and after t=4, and describe in words how P moved.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether it is the change in position or the distance traveled that cancels.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Because P ..., the distance is ...
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say how the change in position and the distance traveled differ?
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that you split the interval where the sign of the velocity changes?
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.model.0: P went in one direction until t=4 and then came back in the opposite direction to the starting point. The changes cancel to 0, but the path covered still remains. So you have to split the interval where the sign of the velocity changes and add the absolute values of the change in each interval.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.model.1: While the velocity is negative it goes forward, then when the velocity becomes positive it changes direction and comes back. The change in position is 0 because of the signs, but the distance is found by calculating the two intervals separately and adding them as positive values.
n-m-h2-integ-03.s.s2.model.2: The movements going and coming have opposite signs, so they cancel in the definite integral. The distance is the integral of |v(t)|, so split where the sign changes and add.

n-m-h2-integ-04.title: Finding the condition for the local minimum value of a function defined by a definite integral
n-m-h2-integ-04.topic: Differentiation and extreme values of functions defined by definite integrals
n-m-h2-integ-04.goal: Use the fact that the increase and decrease and the extreme values of a function F(x)=∫₀ˣ f(t)dt defined by a definite integral are determined by the sign of f(x), to build examples where the local minimum value is positive and find the condition.
n-m-h2-integ-04.material: f(t)=(t−a)(t−b) (a and b are integers with 0<a<b) and F(x)=∫₀ˣ f(t)dt. (∫₀ˣ is the definite integral from 0 to x.)
n-m-h2-integ-04.thinking.0: Reading increase and decrease from F'(x)=f(x)
n-m-h2-integ-04.thinking.1: Distinguishing the location of an extreme value from its size
n-m-h2-integ-04.thinking.2: Finding the condition from several examples
n-m-h2-integ-04.prereq.0: Differentiating a function defined by a definite integral
n-m-h2-integ-04.prereq.1: Increase, decrease, and extreme values of cubic functions
n-m-h2-integ-04.prereq.2: Calculating definite integrals of polynomial functions
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.prompt: For x>0, at which x can F(x) have an extreme value?
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.hint.0: Recall what function you get when you differentiate a function defined by a definite integral.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.hint.1: If you examine the sign of F' on each range of x, you can tell where F is increasing and where it is decreasing.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.o.a: The x where f(x) has an extreme value: F has an extreme value at the same place as f
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.r.a: The increase and decrease of F are determined by the sign of f, not by the value of f. The locations of extreme values of f have nothing to do with extreme values of F.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.o.b: The x where f(x)=0 and the sign of f(x) changes on either side
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.r.b: You used the fact that since F'(x)=f(x), extreme values occur where the sign of F' changes.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.o.c: The x where F(x)=0: an extreme value occurs where the graph crosses the x-axis
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.r.c: The places where F is 0 and the places where extreme values occur are separate matters.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.o.d: x=0: the value of F starts to change at the point where the integration starts
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.r.d: F(0)=0 is just a value, and x=0 is not where the increase and decrease change.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s1.explain: Since F'(x)=f(x)=(x−a)(x−b), F increases for x<a, decreases for a<x<b, and increases for x>b. So F has a local maximum at x=a and a local minimum at x=b.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.prompt: Among integer pairs (a, b) with 0<a<b≤20, enter three different pairs for which the local minimum value of F(x) is positive.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.hint.0: First determine the x where F has its local minimum, then express the value of F at that x in terms of a and b.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.hint.1: Expand and calculate ∫₀ᵇ(t−a)(t−b)dt and work out the condition for the sign to be positive.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers with 0<a<b≤20.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers with 0<a<b≤20.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The local minimum value is positive.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The local minimum value is not positive. Express the value of F at the x where the local minimum occurs in terms of a and b.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s2.explain: The local minimum occurs at x=b, and F(b)=∫₀ᵇ(t²−(a+b)t+ab)dt=b³/3−(a+b)b²/2+ab²=b²(3a−b)/6. Since b²>0, the local minimum value is positive when 3a−b>0, that is, b<3a.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.prompt: Write what relationship there is between b and a in the pairs you found, and explain why that relationship is needed by calculating the local minimum value.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.hint.0: First decide whether the local minimum is at a or b, then expand and calculate the definite integral up to that x.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.hint.1: In the expression you calculated, separate the factors that are always positive from those whose sign can change.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., b is ... than ... of a. The local minimum value is ..., so ...
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you first determine the x where the local minimum occurs and then calculate its value?
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which factor determines the sign of the local minimum value?
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.model.0: b must be less than 3 times a. The local minimum occurs at x=b, and F(b)=b²(3a−b)/6, and since b² is always positive, 3a−b must be positive. So b<3a.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.model.1: When b<3a, the local minimum value is positive. Calculating F(b)=∫₀ᵇ(t−a)(t−b)dt gives b²(3a−b)/6, and its sign is determined by 3a−b.
n-m-h2-integ-04.s.s3.model.2: It is enough that 3a>b. Find the value F(b)=b^2(3a-b)/6 at x=b, where the local minimum occurs, and find the condition for it to be positive: 3a-b>0.

n-m-h2-integ-05.title: Can we find the position from the acceleration alone?
n-m-h2-integ-05.topic: Indefinite integrals and constants of integration: from acceleration to position
n-m-h2-integ-05.goal: Judge that each time you integrate from acceleration to velocity and from velocity to position, one constant of integration appears, so two pieces of information are needed to fix the position, and build different motions that give the same position.
n-m-h2-integ-05.material: The acceleration of a point P moving on a number line at time t (seconds) is a(t)=6t−4. We want to know the position of P at t=3. (Integrating acceleration gives velocity, and integrating velocity gives position.)
n-m-h2-integ-05.thinking.0: Distinguishing the information needed from the information already known
n-m-h2-integ-05.thinking.1: Interpreting what the constant of integration means
n-m-h2-integ-05.thinking.2: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
n-m-h2-integ-05.prereq.0: Indefinite integrals and constants of integration
n-m-h2-integ-05.prereq.1: The relationship among velocity, acceleration, and position
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.prompt: To fix the position of P at t=3, which of the following extra information do we need to know?
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write how many times you must integrate from acceleration to position, and what constant appears each time.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many of those constants the information in each choice can fix. Information already known from the acceleration a(t) is not new information.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.o.a: The velocity at t=0 and the acceleration at t=3
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.r.a: The constant of integration for velocity is fixed, but the one for position remains. The acceleration at t=3 is already known from a(t).
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.o.b: The position at t=0 and the acceleration at t=3
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.r.b: The constant of integration for position is fixed, but the one for velocity remains. The acceleration at t=3 is already known from a(t).
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.o.c: The acceleration at t=1 and the acceleration at t=3
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.r.c: Both values can be calculated from a(t), so there is no new information.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.o.d: The velocity at t=0 and the position at t=0
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.r.d: This is the information that fixes each of the two constants of integration produced by integrating twice.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s1.explain: Integrating a(t) gives v(t)=3t²−4t+C₁, and integrating once more gives x(t)=t³−2t²+C₁t+C₂. Only when both constants of integration C₁ (initial velocity) and C₂ (initial position) are determined is the position fixed.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.prompt: Let v₀ be the velocity at t=0 and x₀ the position. Enter three different pairs of integers (v₀, x₀) such that the position at t=3 is 10. (−20≤v₀≤20, −20≤x₀≤20)
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.hint.0: Integrate twice to find x(t), then plug in t=3 and write it as an expression in v₀ and x₀.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether choosing one v₀ satisfying that expression determines x₀.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.ok.c1: They are integers within the range.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.fail.c1: v₀ and x₀ must be integers from −20 to 20.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The position at t=3 is not 10. Plug t=3 into x(t)=t³−2t²+v₀t+x₀.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s2.explain: x(3)=27−18+3v₀+x₀=9+3v₀+x₀, so x(3)=10 when 3v₀+x₀=1. There are infinitely many (v₀, x₀) satisfying this equation. That is, even with the same position at t=3, there are many motions with different initial velocities and positions.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain why knowing just one position does not let you know both the initial velocity and the initial position, and write why two pieces of information are needed to fix the motion.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many times you integrated to get the position.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the pairs you made earlier all arrive at the same position, and say what is different about them.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If you integrate ... then ... appears, so ...
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that integrating twice produces two constants?
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that if there is only one equation as a condition, (v₀, x₀) is not determined uniquely?
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.model.0: Since we integrate twice from acceleration to position, one constant of integration appears at velocity and one at position. The position at t=3 gives only one equation, such as 3v₀+x₀=1, so v₀ and x₀ are not determined uniquely and many pairs are possible. You need to know both the initial velocity and the initial position.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.model.1: We do not know the 2 constants of integration, but the position at t=3 gives only one equation. So there are infinitely many combinations of initial velocity and initial position. With two constants, you need two pieces of information.
n-m-h2-integ-05.s.s3.model.2: Integrating twice leaves the initial velocity and the initial position each as a constant. A single position value is just one equation tying the two together, so many motions can arrive at the same position.

n-m-h2-integ-06.title: Finding all lines that enclose the same area with a parabola
n-m-h2-integ-06.topic: Area between a parabola and a line: sign and telling above from below
n-m-h2-integ-06.goal: Understand that you must subtract the lower expression from the upper expression to get area, and that the case of a negative slope must be handled in the same way, and find all lines that meet the condition.
n-m-h2-integ-06.material: There is the parabola y=x² and the line y=mx through the origin (m≠0, m is an integer). The two graphs meet at x=0 and x=m. Let S(m) be the area of the enclosed region.
n-m-h2-integ-06.thinking.0: Checking which is above and the interval, using a graph
n-m-h2-integ-06.thinking.1: Checking the direction of the definite integral (lower limit, upper limit) and the sign
n-m-h2-integ-06.prereq.0: Intersection points of a parabola and a line
n-m-h2-integ-06.prereq.1: Area between two curves (upper expression − lower expression)
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct definite integral expression for S(−2) when m=−2.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.hint.0: When m=−2, sketch the two graphs and first mark the x-coordinates of the two intersection points and which graph is above between them.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.hint.1: Recall what happens to the value of a definite integral when the lower limit is greater than the upper limit or when the integrand is negative.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.o.a: ∫₀^{−2}(−2x−x²)dx: integrate from 0 to −2, subtracting the lower expression from the upper expression
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.r.a: The lower limit (0) is greater than the upper limit (−2), so the sign of the value flips. Area cannot be negative.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.o.b: ∫_{−2}^{0}(−2x−x²)dx: integrate from −2 to 0, subtracting the lower expression from the upper expression
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.r.b: This is the correct form, going from the left end to the right end and writing upper expression − lower expression.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.o.c: ∫_{−2}^{0}(x²+2x)dx: integrate from −2 to 0, subtracting the line's expression from the parabola's expression
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.r.c: On this interval the line is above the parabola. If you subtract the upper expression from the lower expression, the value is negative.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.o.d: ∫₀²(−2x−x²)dx: integrate from 0 to 2, subtracting the parabola's expression from the line's expression
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.r.d: When m=−2, the two graphs meet at x=0 and x=−2. The interval is not on the right side of the x-axis.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s1.explain: When m=−2, the two graphs meet at x=−2 and x=0, and for −2<x<0 the line y=−2x is above the parabola y=x². So S(−2)=∫_{−2}^{0}(−2x−x²)dx=4/3.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.prompt: Enter two different integers m such that S(m)=9/2. (−30≤m≤30, m≠0)
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.hint.0: When m is positive, first find S(m) as an expression in m.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.hint.1: When m is negative, draw the graph and compare whether you get the same expression.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.ok.c1: A nonzero integer within the range.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.fail.c1: m must be a nonzero integer from −30 to 30.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.fail.c2: S(m) is not 9/2. First find S(m) as an expression in m for m>0.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s2.explain: If m>0, S(m)=∫₀ᵐ(mx−x²)dx=m³/6. If m<0, thinking of symmetry about the y-axis with −m=|m|, S(m)=|m|³/6. Therefore |m|³=27, that is, m=3 or m=−3.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain why a student who found one value with m>0 could think there is one more line with the same area.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.hint.0: Sketch the graphs for m=3 and m=−3 on the same coordinate plane and see how they are related.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.hint.1: Recall what the axis of symmetry of the parabola y=x² is.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If we ... the line, then ...
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what happens to the area when the graph is flipped about the y-axis?
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the area is positive even if the sign of the slope is different?
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.model.0: If you reflect the shape enclosed by y=x² and the line y=3x across the y-axis, you get the shape enclosed by y=x² and y=−3x. The shape and size are the same, so the area is the same, and m=−3 is also an answer.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.model.1: Even if the slope is negative, the area is positive. The area is determined by the absolute value of m, as in |m|³/6, so m=3 and m=−3 give the same area.
n-m-h2-integ-06.s.s3.model.2: The parabola is symmetric about the y-axis, so changing only the sign of the line's slope just flips the shape left to right and leaves its size unchanged. So the negative slope −3 is also possible.

n-m-h2-integ-07.title: If the derivative of a constant is 0, is k also 0?
n-m-h2-integ-07.topic: The value of a definite integral is a constant: function equations containing a definite integral
n-m-h2-integ-07.goal: Understand that the definite integral ∫₀¹ f(t)dt is a constant unrelated to x but its value is not 0 and must be calculated from the definition, and write a kind explanation to a junior student who made the same error.
n-m-h2-integ-07.material: This is Haeun's solution for finding the function f(x) that satisfies the condition f(x)=x²+2∫₀¹ f(t)dt. (∫₀¹ is the definite integral from 0 to 1.)
n-m-h2-integ-07.thinking.0: Distinguishing "is a constant" from "has the value 0"
n-m-h2-integ-07.thinking.1: Testing a conclusion by checking the answer
n-m-h2-integ-07.thinking.2: Explaining an error while respecting the other person's solution
n-m-h2-integ-07.prereq.2: Choosing a letter in a function equation
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Haeun's solution.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether each line really follows from the one before it, and whether each line has a sufficient reason.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.hint.1: Go back over how k was defined, and think about what happens if you plug the f(x) found at the end into that definition.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.line.0: ∫₀¹ f(t)dt is a value that does not contain x, so letting it be k, f(x)=x²+2k.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.line.1: Differentiating both sides with respect to x gives f'(x)=2x, so k disappears when differentiated.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.line.2: k is a constant and the derivative of a constant is 0, so k=0.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first one that is wrong. It is true that the derivative of a constant is 0, but that does not mean the value of the constant is 0. The value of k must be determined from the definition k=∫₀¹ f(t)dt. Plugging in f(t)=t²+2k gives k=∫₀¹(t²+2k)dt=1/3+2k, so k=−1/3 and f(x)=x²−2/3.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.prompt: What is the most direct way to confirm that Haeun's answer f(x)=x² is wrong?
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.hint.0: Plug f(x)=x² into both sides of the original equation f(x)=x²+2∫₀¹ f(t)dt.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether each check "always comes out right even for a wrong answer."
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.o.a: Differentiate f(x)=x² with respect to x and check that f'(x)=2x
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.r.a: Haeun's solution already satisfies this condition. This check does not reveal the error.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.o.b: Check only that f(0)=0, and see whether it agrees with k=0 from f(0)=0+2k in the original equation
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.r.b: If f(0)=0, it looks consistent with k=0, so no contradiction shows up. Unless you examine k through the value of the definite integral, you cannot catch the error.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.o.c: Plug f(x)=x² into ∫₀¹ f(t)dt, calculate the value, and compare it with k=0
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.r.c: This check calculates the value of the definite integral directly and sees whether it agrees with the definition of k.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.o.d: Check whether using a different letter instead of k gives the same solution
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.r.d: Changing the name of the letter does not change the logic of the solution.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s2.explain: If f(x)=x², then ∫₀¹ t²dt=1/3, so k should be 1/3, but Haeun said k=0. The two do not agree, so f(x)=x² does not satisfy the original condition.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a short note to Haeun. Include one thing she did well, why the wrong line is wrong, and the key of the correct solution and its result.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.hint.0: Find one thing that was right in Haeun's solution, and guess what thinking the wrong line came from.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write down the expression needed to fix the wrong line (the expression that writes k as a definite integral).
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you first say specifically what was done well?
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain that "the derivative of a constant is 0" and "the value of the constant is 0" are different?
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.model.0: Haeun, letting the definite integral be k was a good idea! But "the derivative of a constant is 0" means the result of differentiating is 0, not that the value of k is 0. You have to find k from its definition, k=∫₀¹(t²+2k)dt=1/3+2k, so k=−1/3, and f(x)=x²−2/3.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.model.1: It was very good that you started by letting the value unrelated to x be k. But k being a constant, so that its derivative is 0, is a different matter from k having the value 0. If you calculate the definite integral directly, solving k=1/3+2k gives k=-1/3, so f(x)=x²-2/3.
n-m-h2-integ-07.s.s3.model.2: Haeun, nice work. If you plug the f(x)=x² you found at the end into ∫₀¹ f(t)dt, you get 1/3, which does not agree with k=0. You have to calculate the value of the definite integral to determine k, and then k=−1/3 and f(x)=x²−2/3.

n-m-h2-integ-08.title: If we cut at the middle of the interval, does the area also split in half?
n-m-h2-integ-08.goal: Check and explain, with definite integral calculations and an example you build yourself, that cutting at the middle of an interval does not bisect the area, and that the cutting position is shifted toward the side where the function is larger.
n-m-h2-integ-08.material: There is a figure enclosed by the line y=2x, the x-axis, and the two lines x=1 and x=7. Sua said, "If you draw a vertical line at x=4, the middle of the interval 1≤x≤7, the area is bisected," and Dohyeon said, "Let's check with a definite integral."
n-m-h2-integ-08.thinking.0: Testing an intuitive claim with numbers
n-m-h2-integ-08.thinking.1: Finding a common rule from several examples
n-m-h2-integ-08.thinking.2: Connecting the shape of a graph with the distribution of area
n-m-h2-integ-08.prereq.1: Finding values that satisfy an equation within the integers
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.prompt: How does the vertical line x=4 divide the area of the figure?
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the heights of the left part and the right part of the figure with x=4 as the dividing line.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate and compare the definite integrals of the two parts, ∫₁⁴ 2x dx and ∫₄⁷ 2x dx.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.o.a: It is bisected: because the left and right intervals have the same width
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.r.a: Even with the same width, if the heights differ, the areas differ. On the right interval the line is higher.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.o.b: It is bisected: because it is a line, so the height is constant on any interval
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.r.b: The height of y=2x changes with x. The height is constant only for y=constant.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.o.c: It is not bisected: because the right part is lower, so the left part has the greater area
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.r.c: The line gets higher toward the right, so the right side has the greater area.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.o.d: It is not bisected: because the height increases toward the right, so the right part is greater
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.r.d: You used the fact that more area piles up on the side where the height is greater.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s1.explain: ∫₁⁴ 2x dx=16−1=15 and ∫₄⁷ 2x dx=49−16=33. The left is 15 and the right is 33, so it is not bisected, and the right is greater.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.prompt: Enter two different integer triples (a, b, k) such that the vertical line x=k exactly bisects the area between y=2x, the x-axis, and the two vertical lines x=a and x=b. (1≤a<k<b≤50)
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the definite integrals of the left part and the right part of x=k in terms of a, b, k.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.hint.1: Simplify the equation saying the two values are equal and test combinations of integers.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The areas to the left and right of x=k are equal.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The left area and the right area are not equal. Express ∫ₐᵏ 2x dx and ∫ₖᵇ 2x dx in terms of a, b, k.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s2.explain: ∫ₐᵏ 2x dx=k²−a² and ∫ₖᵇ 2x dx=b²−k², so k²−a²=b²−k², that is, 2k²=a²+b². For example, (1, 7, 5) gives 25−1=24=49−25.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.prompt: In the triples you found, is k greater or less than the middle (average) of a and b? Explain why, connecting it to the shape of y=2x.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each triple you found, find the average (a+b)/2 and compare it with k.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.hint.1: Recall which side has the greater area when you cut at the middle.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., k is ... than the middle. This is because ...
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the areas of the left part and the right part at the middle?
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say, with a reason, which way the bisecting position is shifted?
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.model.0: k is greater than the average. The line gets higher toward the right, so if you cut at the middle, the right area is greater. So to split the area in half, you have to move the cutting line to the right of the middle.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.model.1: In (1,7,5), the average is 4 but k=5, so k is greater. More area piles up on the side where the height is greater, so the bisecting line is shifted to the right.
n-m-h2-integ-08.s.s3.model.2: The k that bisects is to the right of the midpoint of a and b. This is because y=2x is higher on the right, so if you cut at the middle, the right part is greater.

n-m-h2-integ-09.title: Can we find the area easily even if the shape is complicated?
n-m-h2-integ-09.topic: Area between two curves: the difference in height
n-m-h2-integ-09.goal: Understand that the area between two curves, one of which is the other shifted up, is determined only by the difference in height and the width of the interval, and in the same way build examples that meet a condition and a new problem.
n-m-h2-integ-09.material: There is the curve y=x³−3x and the curve y=x³−3x+4, which is that curve shifted up by 4. We want to find the area between the two curves on the interval 0≤x≤3. (On this interval, the first curve also has a part that goes below the x-axis.)
n-m-h2-integ-09.thinking.0: Reducing the calculation by looking at the structure (the difference) of the expressions
n-m-h2-integ-09.thinking.1: Not being tied to the relationship with the x-axis
n-m-h2-integ-09.thinking.2: Making a problem that meets the conditions yourself
n-m-h2-integ-09.prereq.0: Area between two curves = ∫(upper expression − lower expression)
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct judgment about the area between the two curves.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.hint.0: Decide which of the two curves is above, and subtract the lower expression from the upper expression.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.hint.1: Simplify the expression after subtracting and see what expression you get.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.o.a: 12: the height difference is constant at 4 everywhere, so multiply by the width 3
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.r.a: You used the structure that the upper expression minus the lower expression is constant at 4.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.o.b: 4: the two curves are 4 apart, so that value is the area
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.r.b: The difference in height is 4, but for area you must also multiply by the width of the interval.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.o.c: 0: the first curve goes below the x-axis, becomes negative, and cancels
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.r.c: The area between two curves is determined by upper expression − lower expression, not by the relationship with the x-axis. This difference is always positive.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell: we have to calculate the definite integral of x³−3x first
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.r.d: In upper expression − lower expression, x³−3x cancels out, so no calculation is needed.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s1.explain: Subtracting the lower curve from the upper curve gives (x³−3x+4)−(x³−3x)=4. So the area is ∫₀³ 4 dx=12. The position of the curves relative to the x-axis does not matter.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.prompt: Enter three different pairs of natural numbers (k, w) such that the area between the curve y=x² and the curve y=x²+k, which is it shifted up by k, is exactly 24 on the interval 0≤x≤w. (1≤k≤24, 1≤w≤24)
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.hint.0: First write the difference in height between the two curves as an expression.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.hint.1: Integrate that difference from 0 to w, write it in terms of k and w, and compare it with 24.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.ok.c1: They are natural numbers within the range.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.fail.c1: k and w must be natural numbers from 1 to 24.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The area between the two curves is 24.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The area is not 24. First simplify (upper expression − lower expression).
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s2.explain: Since (x²+k)−x²=k, the area is ∫₀ʷ k dx=kw. The pairs of natural numbers with kw=24 are (1,24), (2,12), (3,8), (4,6), (6,4), (8,3), (12,2), (24,1). The shape of the curve x² does not affect the answer.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.prompt: This time, choose the curve y=g(x) yourself. Write, in one sentence, a problem in which the area between two curves is 18, and explain why that problem can be solved without finding the definite integral of g(x).
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.hint.0: It is easy to make the problem if you first choose two numbers whose product (height difference times interval width) is 18, and then pick the curve.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.hint.1: Subtract the expressions of the two curves and check what happens to g(x).
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Problem: ... Solution: the height difference is ... and the width is ..., so ...
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your problem include both curves and the interval?
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that when you subtract the two expressions, g(x) disappears?
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.model.0: Problem: Find the area between the curves y=x³−x and y=x³−x+3 on 0≤x≤6. The height difference between the two curves is constant at 3 everywhere and the width of the interval is 6, so the area is 3×6=18, and there is no need to integrate x³−x.
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.model.1: Problem: What is the area enclosed by y=2x² and y=2x²+2 on 1≤x≤10? Subtracting the lower expression from the upper leaves only 2, so the height difference is always 2. Multiplying by the width 9 gives 18, so you do not need to integrate g(x).
n-m-h2-integ-09.s.s3.model.2: If you choose g(x)=x³−5x and make a problem asking for the area between it and the curve shifted up by 1 on 0≤x≤18, the height difference is constantly 1 and the width is 18, so the area is 18. This is because g disappears when you subtract.

n-m-h2-integ-10.title: Is the area estimated with rectangles greater or less than the real one?
n-m-h2-integ-10.topic: The meaning of the definite integral: estimating area with rectangles
n-m-h2-integ-10.goal: Understand, by revising your judgment as information is revealed, that whether the value estimated with rectangles is greater or less than the real area depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.
n-m-h2-integ-10.material: We estimate with rectangles the area A of the figure (0≤x≤1) enclosed by the curve y=x², the x-axis, and the line x=1. Divide the interval into n equal parts and build a rectangle on each piece. If the height is the value measured at the left end of each piece, it is the "left sum," and if it is the value measured at the right end, it is the "right sum."
n-m-h2-integ-10.thinking.0: Revising your judgment each time new information appears
n-m-h2-integ-10.thinking.1: Connecting where the height is measured with whether the curve is increasing or decreasing
n-m-h2-integ-10.thinking.2: Examining whether the estimates enclose the real value from above and below
n-m-h2-integ-10.prereq.0: The meaning of a definite integral as area
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose a judgment using only the information revealed.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece, draw and compare whether the top side of the rectangle is above or below the curve.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.hint.1: At the place where the height is measured (left end, right end), compare whether the height of the curve is the lowest or the highest within the piece.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.info: When n=2, the left sum is (1/2)×(0²+(1/2)²)=0.125 and the right sum is (1/2)×((1/2)²+1²)=0.625.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can we say about the real area A?
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.after: This curve gets higher toward the right, so the left sum is less than the real value and the right sum is greater than the real value. The real area A is between the two values.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A is between 0.125 and 0.625: the left sum falls short and the right sum overshoots
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You used the fact that since the curve rises to the right, in each piece the height at the left end is the lowest and the height at the right end is the highest.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A is 0.375: because the average of the two values is always the real area
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There is no guarantee that the average equals the real area. It depends on the shape of the curve.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A is greater than 0.625: because the rectangles fill only below the curve
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The rectangles of the right sum stick out above the curve. It is the left sum that fills only below the curve.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.info: When we increased to n=4, the left sum became 0.21875 and the right sum became 0.46875.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: What happens between the two sums and the real area A if we increase n further?
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.after: As n gets larger, the width shrinks and the difference between the two sums shrinks. So the definite integral can be thought of as the value squeezed between the two sums.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The two sums get closer toward A, and A stays between the two values
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You confirmed that the two sums narrow and enclose A from above and below.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The left sum decreases and the right sum increases, moving away from A
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: From n=2 to 4, the left sum increased and the right sum decreased.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: At some point the two sums cross over, and A falls outside them
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: As long as the curve keeps rising, the left sum is always smaller and the right sum is always greater, so A is between the two values.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.info: This time, we estimated the curve y=1−x² (0≤x≤1) in the same way with n=2, and the left sum was 0.875, the right sum was 0.375, and the real area was about 0.667.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: Why is the left sum greater than the real area for this curve?
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.after: Which direction the estimate goes, greater or less, depending on where you measure the height, depends on whether the curve is increasing or decreasing. For a decreasing curve, the direction is reversed.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is a calculation mistake: because the left sum always comes out smaller than the real area
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Always coming out smaller holds only when the curve rises.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The curve goes down, so the left end is the highest and the rectangles overshoot the curve
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You thought about how the left sum becomes greater or smaller depending on whether the curve is increasing or decreasing.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The curve has a part that goes below the x-axis, so the sign is reversed
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: On 0≤x≤1, 1−x² is at least 0, so it does not go below the x-axis.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s1.reflect: At first the rule that the left sum is small and the right sum is large seemed to hold always, but when the curve went down, it reversed. Whether an estimate is greater or less than the real value is determined by whether the curve is increasing or decreasing.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.prompt: Write what condition the curve (function) must satisfy for us to say that the left sum is always less than or equal to the real area, and give one example for when that condition is missing.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.hint.0: Explain why the left sum is small using where the height is measured and the height of the curve.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether that reason also works when the curve goes down.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Only when the curve ... For example, ...
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you connect where the height is measured with whether the curve is increasing or decreasing?
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: In the example where the condition fails, did you say which way the estimate goes wrong?
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.model.0: The curve must keep increasing on the interval for the left sum to be less than or equal to the real area. For example, for a decreasing curve such as y=1−x², the left end is the highest, so the left sum is greater than the real area.
n-m-h2-integ-10.s.s2.model.1: It holds only on intervals where the function rises. For a curve that goes down, for example y=4−x², it is the opposite: the left sum overshoots and the right sum falls short.

n-m-h2-limit-01.title: What do we need to know to say a function is continuous?
n-m-h2-limit-01.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the conditions for continuity
n-m-h2-limit-01.goal: Sort out what information is necessary and sufficient to conclude that a function is continuous at x=a, determine for yourself whether a function is continuous, and organize that criterion in your own words.
n-m-h2-limit-01.material: We want to find out whether a function f is continuous at x=1. The left-hand limit is the value f(x) approaches as x approaches 1 from the side where x is less than 1, and the right-hand limit is the value it approaches from the side where x is greater than 1. Think about whether we can conclude "it is continuous" when we know only part of the information.
n-m-h2-limit-01.thinking.0: Distinguishing the information that lets us conclude from the information that falls short
n-m-h2-limit-01.thinking.1: Examining the relationships among the function value, the left-hand limit, and the right-hand limit
n-m-h2-limit-01.thinking.2: Organizing the criterion for judging in words
n-m-h2-limit-01.prereq.0: The meaning of left-hand and right-hand limits
n-m-h2-limit-01.prereq.1: Experience distinguishing function values from limit values
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one piece of information, among the following about f, that lets you be certain that f is continuous at x=1 when you know only that one piece.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.hint.0: First list what you must check in order to say it is continuous, and then mark whether each choice satisfies all of them.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.hint.1: Distinguish "the value is defined" and "that value equals the limit value" as different pieces of information.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.o.a: f(1)=3, and f(x) approaches 3 as x approaches 1 from the greater side
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.r.a: You looked at only one one-sided limit. We do not yet know the value when approaching from the other side.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.o.b: f(1)=3, and the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and are equal to each other
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.r.b: You know the limit exists, but you cannot tell whether that limit value equals f(1)=3.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.o.c: f(1)=3, and the left-hand and right-hand limits are both 3
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.o.d: The left-hand and right-hand limits are both 3, and f(1) is defined as some value
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.r.d: Knowing only that f(1) is defined, you cannot tell whether that value is 3.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s1.explain: For continuity, f(1) must be defined, the limit as x→1 must exist, and that limit value must equal f(1). Choice c satisfies all three. Choice a has only a one-sided limit, b does not connect the limit with f(1), and d does not know the value of f(1), so we cannot tell whether it equals the limit value.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.prompt: Select all of the following four functions that are continuous at x=1.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.hint.0: For each function, find in turn the function value at x=1, the left-hand limit, and the right-hand limit, and organize them in a table.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.hint.1: For a fractional expression, simplify it for x≠1, then find the value as x approaches 1.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.r.b: As x→1, (x²−1)/(x−1)=x+1 approaches 2, but f₂(1)=1, so the limit value and the function value differ.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.r.c: If there is no function value at x=1, we cannot call it continuous even if the limit exists.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s2.explain: f₁ equals x+1 for x≠1, so its limit is 2, and f₁(1)=2 matches. For f₄, the left-hand limit is 2, the right-hand limit is 3·1−1=2, and f₄(1)=2, so all are equal. For f₂, the limit value 2 and the function value 1 differ, and f₃ has no f₃(1).
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.prompt: In s2, the functions that are not continuous were eliminated for different reasons. In your own words, organize what you must check to say that a function is continuous at x=a.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write again on which item each of f₂ and f₃ was eliminated.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.hint.1: If the reasons they were rejected are different, count how many things you need to check to rule them all out.
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state all three conditions without leaving any out?
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do your criteria include the reasons that f₂ and f₃ were rejected?
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.model.0: f is continuous at x=a if f(a) is defined, the limit exists because the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal as x→a, and that limit equals f(a).
n-m-h2-limit-01.s.s3.model.1: First, the function value must exist. Second, the limit must exist, meaning the limits from both sides are equal. Third, that limit must equal the function value.

n-m-h2-limit-02.title: Checking a claim that a root exists by the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-02.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-02.goal: When using the Intermediate Value Theorem, do not look only at signs: check that the conditions of the theorem are satisfied, and show with a counterexample that the claim is false.
n-m-h2-limit-02.material: Seojin wanted to find out whether the equation 1/x=0 has a real root in the interval (−1, 2), so she set f(x)=1/x and worked as follows.
n-m-h2-limit-02.thinking.0: Checking the assumptions before using a theorem
n-m-h2-limit-02.thinking.1: Finding the line where a condition of the theorem is missing
n-m-h2-limit-02.thinking.2: Choosing a way to supply the missing condition
n-m-h2-limit-02.prereq.0: Continuous functions and the statement of the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-02.prereq.1: The domain of the rational function y=1/x
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Seojin's solution.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into "calculation" or "judgment that applies the theorem."
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.hint.1: For the line that applies the theorem, compare the conditions the theorem requires with what was checked, one by one.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.line.0: Let f(x)=1/x. Then f(−1)=−1 and f(2)=1/2.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.line.2: By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there exists c between −1 and 2 with f(c)=0.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the equation 1/x=0 has a real root in the interval (−1, 2).
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first mistake. The Intermediate Value Theorem can be used only when f is continuous on the closed interval [−1, 2], but f(x)=1/x is not defined at x=0, which lies inside this interval. The calculations in lines 1 and 2 are correct, and line 4 just follows the wrong conclusion of line 3.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.prompt: Show that Seojin's conclusion is wrong. Write what condition a function must satisfy for the Intermediate Value Theorem to be used, why f(x)=1/x does not satisfy it, and what the real roots of 1/x=0 actually are.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the theorem in the form "if ..., then ..." and count how many conditions come after "if."
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the domain of f(x)=1/x is missing any point between −1 and 2.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the condition of the theorem (continuity) first?
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you point out that x=0 lies inside the interval?
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.model.0: The Intermediate Value Theorem can be used only when f is continuous on [−1, 2]. But f(x)=1/x is not defined at x=0, so it is not continuous. In fact, no x satisfies 1/x=0, so there is no real root.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s2.model.1: To use the theorem, the function must be continuous on the interval, but 1/x breaks at x=0, so it cannot be used. Because the numerator is 1, there is no x for which 1/x is 0, so this equation has no solution.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.prompt: Keep f(−1)<0<f(2) as it is. Choose the condition that must be added to conclude for certain that f(x)=0 has a root in the interval (−1, 2).
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine whether a graph that jumps or has a break inside the interval could skip over 0 without passing through it.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.hint.1: Decide whether each option is about the endpoints or about the whole interval.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.o.a: f is continuous at x=−1 and at x=2
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.r.a: Even if f is continuous only at the two ends, a break in the middle of the interval can make you miss a root.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.o.b: f(−1) and f(2) are both integers
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.r.b: Whether the values are integers has nothing to do with whether a root exists.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.o.c: f is continuous at every point of the closed interval [−1, 2]
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.o.d: f(x) is nonzero for every x in the interval (−1, 2)
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.r.d: This means there is no root, so it actually contradicts the conclusion.
n-m-h2-limit-02.s.s3.explain: The Intermediate Value Theorem requires continuity on the whole closed interval. With this condition, 0 must occur between endpoint values of opposite signs.

n-m-h2-limit-03.title: The relationship between the signs of the endpoint values and a root inside the interval
n-m-h2-limit-03.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the converse of the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-03.goal: Distinguish what the Intermediate Value Theorem gives (a sufficient condition) from what it does not give, and build and check an example where the converse of the theorem does not hold.
n-m-h2-limit-03.material: For a continuous function f, the Intermediate Value Theorem says, "If f(0)f(4)<0, then there is an x in the interval (0, 4) with f(x)=0." Doyun claims, "Then when f(0)f(4)>0, there will be no root in (0, 4)."
n-m-h2-limit-03.thinking.0: Deciding the shape of a counterexample
n-m-h2-limit-03.thinking.1: Building several examples that satisfy the conditions
n-m-h2-limit-03.thinking.2: Stating the direction of the theorem (sufficient condition)
n-m-h2-limit-03.prereq.0: The Intermediate Value Theorem for continuous functions
n-m-h2-limit-03.prereq.1: Graphs of quadratic functions and the location of roots
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.prompt: To show Doyun's claim is false, what kind of continuous function should you look for?
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write Doyun's claim split into "assumption → conclusion."
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what the assumption and the conclusion must each be for the claim to be false.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.o.a: A continuous function with f(0)f(4)<0 and no root in (0, 4)
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.r.a: Because of the Intermediate Value Theorem, such a function cannot exist. If the theorem is correct, you cannot find one.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.o.b: A continuous function with f(0)f(4)>0 and no root in (0, 4)
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.r.b: This example agrees with Doyun's claim, so it does not break the claim.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.o.c: A continuous function with f(0)f(4)<0 and a root in (0, 4)
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.r.c: This is a case the theorem guarantees, so it has nothing to do with the claim.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.o.d: A continuous function with f(0)f(4)>0 and a root in (0, 4)
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s1.explain: To show that a claim of the form "if ..., then ..." is false, you need an example that satisfies the assumption but fails the conclusion, that is, an example with a root in (0, 4) even though f(0)f(4)>0.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.prompt: Let f(x)=(x−a)(x−b). Enter two different pairs (a, b) such that f(0)f(4)>0 and f(x)=0 has two distinct real roots in the interval (0, 4). (a<b)
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write f(0) and f(4) in terms of a and b, and work out where the roots must be for the two values to have the same sign.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one root in the interval (0, 4), an integer or a decimal, then pick the other root between that root and the edge of the interval, and check it by direct calculation.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.fail.c3: A root lies outside the interval (0, 4).
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.explain: f(0)=ab and f(4)=(4−a)(4−b), and if both roots lie between 0 and 4, both are positive. So even though f(0)f(4)>0, there are two roots in (0, 4). The graph dips below the x-axis and then comes back up.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Even with such an example, the Intermediate Value Theorem is not wrong. Explain why in one or two sentences.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Rewrite which direction the theorem states: what implies what.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about whether the sentence with that direction reversed means the same thing.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you state the direction of the theorem accurately in words?
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show that the example does not contradict the theorem?
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.model.0: The Intermediate Value Theorem only says that if the signs differ, there is a root. It does not say there is no root when the signs are the same, so a graph that crosses the x-axis twice does not contradict the theorem.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.model.1: The converse of the theorem is not guaranteed. Even if the endpoint values have the same sign, the graph can cross the x-axis in the middle and come back, so a root can exist.
