n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.model.2: The theorem says only "if the signs differ, there is a root." It does not say "if there is a root, the signs differ."
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s2.because.model.3: What the theorem says goes only as far as "if the signs differ, there is a root." It does not mean that this is the only case in which a root exists.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the functions below for which the Intermediate Value Theorem alone lets you conclude for certain that there is an x in the interval (0, 4) with f(x)=0.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.hint.0: For each function, check both the signs of f(0) and f(4) and whether there is any break in [0, 4].
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write down which two things the theorem needs to be satisfied in order to guarantee a root, and compare each option against them.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.r.a: f(0)=4 and f(4)=4 have the same sign, so the assumption of the theorem is not satisfied. Even if x=2 is a root, this theorem did not guarantee it.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.r.c: The signs of f(0) and f(4) differ, but f is not continuous at x=2, so the theorem cannot be used. In fact, there is no root either.
n-m-h2-limit-03.s.s3.explain: For b, f(0)=−1 and f(4)=3, and it is a polynomial function, hence continuous, so the theorem guarantees a root. The same holds for d, where f(0)=−3 and f(4)=5 and f is continuous. For a, f(0)=4 and f(4)=4 have the same sign, so the theorem cannot be used (the root x=2 exists, but the theorem does not guarantee it). For c, the signs differ, but f breaks at x=2 and is not continuous, so the theorem cannot be used.

n-m-h2-limit-04.title: The limit of a composite function: examining Mina's claim
n-m-h2-limit-04.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the limit of a composite function
n-m-h2-limit-04.goal: Using an example, confirm that the limit of a composite function changes depending on the side from which the inner function approaches 0, and explain whether the claim is true or false, giving reasons.
n-m-h2-limit-04.material: Define the function f by f(t)=1 (t>0), f(0)=0, f(t)=−1 (t<0). As t→0, the left-hand limit −1 and the right-hand limit 1 are different, so the limit of f does not exist. Suppose the function g gets close to 0 as x→0. Mina says, "Then the limit of the composite function f(g(x)) as x→0 does not exist either." (Consider only x with g(x)≠0.)
n-m-h2-limit-04.thinking.0: Choosing an example to test the claim
n-m-h2-limit-04.thinking.1: Describing the situation of approaching from one side
n-m-h2-limit-04.thinking.2: Sorting out what to look at when deciding whether a limit exists
n-m-h2-limit-04.prereq.1: The meaning of a composite function
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all of the following choices of g(x) for which the limit of f(g(x)) as x→0 exists.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.hint.0: Replace x with 0.1, −0.1, 0.01, −0.01 and look at the sign of g(x).
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.hint.1: Once the sign of g(x) is determined, check whether the value of f(g(x)) is determined as a single value.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.r.b: If x>0 then g>0, and if x<0 then g<0, so f(g(x)) alternates between 1 and −1.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.r.d: The sign of g changes with the sign of x, so f(g(x)) alternates between 1 and −1.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s1.explain: g(x)=x² (x≠0) is always positive, so f(g(x))=1 and the limit is 1. g(x)=−x⁴ (x≠0) is always negative, so f(g(x))=−1 and the limit is −1. x³ and 2x change sign, so the limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.prompt: Is Mina's statement always true? Decide whether it is true or not, and explain the reason by connecting it to the way g(x) approaches 0.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put the g from s1 that had a limit next to the g that did not, and compare how the sign of g(x) differed.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether it is the size of t or some property of t that determines the value of f(t).
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you give one specific g(x)?
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the side from which it approaches 0 with the value of f?
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.model.0: Mina's statement is not always true. If g(x)=x², then g(x) approaches 0 only from the positive side, so f(g(x)) stays equal to 1 and the limit exists and equals 1.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s2.model.1: No. If g(x) approaches 0 only from the negative side, then f(g(x))=−1 is constant, so the limit exists, and g(x)=−x⁴ is a counterexample.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.prompt: To know whether the limit of f(g(x)) as x→0 exists, what should you examine?
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.hint.0: As x approaches 0, write down which values the input g(x) to f takes near 0.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.hint.1: Sort those values into those on the left-hand-limit side of f and those on the right-hand-limit side.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.o.a: Whether the left-hand and right-hand limits of f(t) as t→0 approach the same single value
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.r.a: Looking only at this leads to the same conclusion as Mina. It does not look at the side from which the inner function approaches.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.o.b: Whether f(0) and g(0) are equal, and whether both are defined
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.r.b: The value at x=0 is not used when finding the limit as x→0.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.o.c: How fast g(x) changes as x approaches 0, and its size
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.r.c: Speed has nothing to do with whether the limit exists.
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.o.d: The sign of the values g(x) takes near 0, and the value of f at that sign
n-m-h2-limit-04.s.s3.explain: The value of f(g(x)) is determined by which side the values of g(x) lie on near 0. If g(x) approaches from one side only, you need the limit from that side. If it approaches from both sides, you must compare the left and right limits.

n-m-h2-limit-05.title: The value of sin(π/x) as x gets close to 0
n-m-h2-limit-05.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the existence of a limit
n-m-h2-limit-05.goal: Do not conclude about a limit from just a few values found in a table. Revise your judgment each time you get more values, and explain why the limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-05.material: For f(x)=sin(π/x) (x≠0), you want to find out what value f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to 0. Add values to the table one at a time and make a judgment. (Use sin kπ=0, sin(π/2)=1, sin(3π/2)=−1.)
n-m-h2-limit-05.thinking.0: Making a tentative judgment from observed values
n-m-h2-limit-05.thinking.1: Revising the judgment when new values appear
n-m-h2-limit-05.thinking.2: Stating the grounds for the nonexistence of a limit
n-m-h2-limit-05.prereq.1: Values of sin (sin kπ=0, sin(π/2)=1, etc.)
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment based only on what you know so far.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.hint.0: Each time a new value appears, compare whether it approaches the same value as the earlier ones.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the way you chose x represents every way of approaching 0.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.info: At x=1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/10, the values of f(x) are all 0. (x gets closer and closer to 0.)
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think about the limit of f(x) as x→0?
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.after: At x of the form 1/n, sin(nπ)=0, so the value is 0. But this may be a result of choosing x in a special way.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I guess it is 0: because the values keep being 0
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the first judgment that comes to mind from only the values seen now.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is too early to conclude before seeing more values of x
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You took into account that you have only some of the values.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There is no limit: because the values are just all the same
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The values being constant is, if anything, a clue that a limit exists.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.info: This time, at x=2/5, 2/9, 2/13, 2/101, the values of f(x) are all 1.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Even as x gets close to 0, f(x) is sometimes 0 and sometimes 1. If a limit exists, f(x) must approach a single value as x gets close to 0.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is still 0: because the first values were 0
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You ignored the new information. Even though x is close to 0, points with value 1 have appeared.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is 1: because the value just seen is 1
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You followed only the most recent value. The 0 seen earlier also came from x close to 0, in the same way.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Hard to say it is a single value: because both 0 and 1 appeared for x close to 0
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You took into account that both values appear.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.info: At x=2/3, 2/7, 2/11, 2/103, the values of f(x) are all −1.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Finally, what can you say about the limit of f(x) as x→0?
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.after: Depending on how x is chosen close to 0, f(x) takes the values 0, 1, and −1, so it cannot be said to approach a single value. The limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The limit does not exist: because 0, 1, and −1 keep appearing for x close to 0
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Having come first is not a reason.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is −1: because it is the last value seen
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You picked the value seen last.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s1.reflect: At first the values kept being 0, so the limit seemed to be 0, but when I looked at other x approaching 0, my judgment changed. A limit must be judged not by "a few values of x" but by whether f approaches the same value for all x approaching 0.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.prompt: Write what to be careful about when guessing a limit from a few values in a table, and the grounds for saying that this function has no limit.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare side by side the x values for which the table showed 0, 1, and −1.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write what must happen to the values if the limit exists, no matter how x approaches 0.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you give specific x values showing that the value differs depending on how x approaches 0?
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why a few values in the table are not enough?
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.model.0: When I chose x only of the form 1/n, I always got 0, but when x approaches 0 in other ways, I get 1 or −1. Depending on the x approaching 0, f takes different values, so there is no limit. You must not decide from just a few values.
n-m-h2-limit-05.s.s2.model.1: Judging from just a few values in the table can lead you wrong. Depending on how x is chosen close to 0, f(x) takes different values 0, 1, and −1, so it does not approach a single value and there is no limit.

n-m-h2-limit-06.title: Writing an explanation of a "broken graph" for Seoyun
n-m-h2-limit-06.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: continuity on the domain
n-m-h2-limit-06.goal: Sort out when the intuition that "a broken graph means discontinuous" is right and when it is off, and explain again in words suitable for a middle-school sibling, connecting it to the domain.
n-m-h2-limit-06.material: Your middle-school sibling Seoyun said, "The graph of f(x)=1/x is broken at x=0, so it is a discontinuous function. A continuous function is one you can draw without lifting your pencil." You want to explain to Seoyun where this goes wrong.
n-m-h2-limit-06.thinking.1: Understanding the relationship between breaks in a graph and the domain
n-m-h2-limit-06.thinking.2: Rewriting an explanation to suit the listener
n-m-h2-limit-06.prereq.0: The definition of continuity (limit value = function value)
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all of the following functions that are continuous at every point of their domain.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write the domain first, then work in this order: for each point in the domain, check whether the limit value equals the function value.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s1.hint.1: Tell whether a place where the graph looks broken is a point inside the domain or outside it.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s1.r.d: At x=0 the left-hand limit is 0, the right-hand limit is 1, and the function value is 1, so the function is not continuous at x=0, a point in the domain.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s1.explain: At every point x≠0, the expression near that point for 1/x and x/|x| is a simple expression in x (1/x, or the constants 1 and −1), so they are continuous at each point of the domain. |x| is continuous at every real number. k is not continuous at x=0, which belongs to the domain, because its left-hand and right-hand limits differ.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.prompt: Write the explanation you would send to Seoyun in 3 to 4 sentences. Seoyun is in middle school and may be hearing words like "limit" and "domain" for the first time. It must include why the break of 1/x is not the same as being a discontinuous function.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.hint.0: Start by writing, in words Seoyun can understand, what happens when you put x=0 into 1/x.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether "the graph is broken" and "the value suddenly jumps at a point where there is a value" mean the same thing.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write it in words a middle-school student can understand?
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you point out the cause of the break accurately (outside the domain)?
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.model.0: Seoyun, 1/x has no value at x=0 at all, so the graph looks broken there. Continuity asks, at each point that has a value, whether the value breaks near that point. Wherever 1/x has a value it does not break, so it is a continuous function.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.model.1: You cannot put 0 into 1/x, so there is no graph at that point at all. A continuous function is one whose limit value equals its function value at every point where it is defined, so 1/x, which does not break at the points where it has values, is also a continuous function.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.model.2: Seoyun, you cannot put 0 into 1/x. So there is no point of the graph at x=0 at all. There is no break anywhere the graph is drawn, so it is a continuous function.
n-m-h2-limit-06.s.s2.model.3: Seoyun, you can't divide by 0, right? So 1/x is simply not drawn at 0. Where it is drawn there is no sudden break, so we call it a continuous function.

n-m-h2-limit-07.title: Building the continuity of a sum of two functions yourself
n-m-h2-limit-07.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: the sum of continuous functions
n-m-h2-limit-07.goal: Check the direction of the property that a sum of continuous functions is continuous, and build for yourself a pair of functions whose sum is continuous but which are each discontinuous, then explain why.
n-m-h2-limit-07.material: You learned that if two functions f and g are continuous at x=0, then f+g is also continuous at x=0. You want to find out whether the various flipped versions of this property are all true.
n-m-h2-limit-07.thinking.0: Telling the direction of a property
n-m-h2-limit-07.thinking.1: Building an example that satisfies the conditions
n-m-h2-limit-07.thinking.2: Explaining why the discontinuities cancel each other
n-m-h2-limit-07.prereq.0: The definition of continuity at x=a
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.prompt: For two functions f and g, choose all of the following that are always true.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.hint.0: In each statement, separate the assumption from the conclusion, and mark whether it has the same direction as the property you learned or the reverse.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.hint.1: You can test the reversed statements with two simple step functions.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.o.a: If f and g are continuous at x=0, then f+g is continuous at x=0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.o.b: If f+g is continuous at x=0, then both f and g are continuous at x=0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.r.b: This is the reverse-direction claim. Think about whether f and g can make up for each other's discontinuity.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.o.c: If f and g are discontinuous at x=0, then f+g is discontinuous at x=0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether two discontinuities can disappear when combined.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.o.d: If f and g are continuous at x=0, then f·g is continuous at x=0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s1.explain: A sum and a product of continuous functions are continuous, so a and d are true. For b and c, there are cases where they do not hold. In s2, build such examples yourself and check.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.prompt: With two constants p and q, form the functions f(x)=1 (x≥0), f(x)=p (x<0) and g(x)=1 (x≥0), g(x)=q (x<0). Enter two different pairs (p, q) for which f and g are both discontinuous at x=0 but f+g is continuous at x=0.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value of f+g at x=0 in terms of p and q.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the relationship between p and q that makes all three values equal, and choose a pair that does not have p=1 or q=1.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.var.p: The value p of f for x<0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.var.q: The value q of g for x<0
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.fail.c1: If p=1, then f is continuous.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.fail.c2: If q=1, then g is continuous.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The left-hand limit of f+g differs from its function value.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.explain: At x=0, the right-hand limit and function value of f+g are 1+1=2, and the left-hand limit is p+q. So f+g is continuous when p+q=2. If p=1 or q=1, one of the functions is already continuous, so those are excluded.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why f+g is continuous even though f and g are each discontinuous.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the difference between the left-hand limit and the function value of f at x=0, and the same difference for g.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check what happens when you add the two differences.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the size of each function's mismatch as an expression?
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show that the mismatch becomes 0 when they are combined?
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.model.0: At x=0, f jumps by p−1 downward and g by q−1, but when combined they cancel out, so the left-hand limit of f+g is 2, and the right-hand limit and function value are also 2, so it is continuous.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s2.because.model.1: Adding the left-hand limits gives p+q=2, so the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value of f+g are all equal to 2. The mismatches of the two functions combine and disappear.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.prompt: Using the same frame as in s2 (1 for x≥0, p or q for x<0), you want to build an example where "the product f·g is continuous at x=0 but f and g are both discontinuous." Which condition is appropriate?
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.hint.0: First find the right-hand limit and function value of the product f·g at x=0.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write the left-hand limit in terms of p and q, then make an equation saying it equals the earlier value.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.r.a: You carried over the condition for the sum. For the product, the left-hand limit is pq.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.r.c: You did not check that the right-hand limit and function value of the product are 1·1=1.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.r.d: p=q alone does not give pq=1. For example, if p=q=2, then pq=4.
n-m-h2-limit-07.s.s3.explain: At x=0, the right-hand limit and function value of f·g are 1·1=1, and the left-hand limit is pq. So it is continuous when pq=1. If p≠1, then q=1/p≠1, so both functions are discontinuous (for example, p=2, q=1/2).

n-m-h2-limit-08.title: Checking a limit solution involving |x−1|
n-m-h2-limit-08.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: limits of expressions with absolute values
n-m-h2-limit-08.goal: Realize that you must consider signs before cancelling in an expression with an absolute value, and fix the solution by finding the left-hand and right-hand limits separately.
n-m-h2-limit-08.material: Hyunwoo found the value of lim_{x→1} (x²−1)/|x−1| as follows. (|x−1| is the absolute value of x−1.)
n-m-h2-limit-08.thinking.0: Finding the first line that goes wrong in the solution
n-m-h2-limit-08.thinking.1: Fixing the solution with left-hand and right-hand limits
n-m-h2-limit-08.thinking.2: Checking the sign of the expression inside an absolute value
n-m-h2-limit-08.prereq.0: The meaning of left-hand and right-hand limits
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Hyunwoo's solution.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write |x−1| without the absolute value symbol for x less than 1 and for x greater than 1.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that result with the expression Hyunwoo cancelled.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s1.line.1: Cancelling x−1 in the numerator and denominator gives x+1.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first mistake. The denominator is |x−1|, not x−1, so for x<1, |x−1|=−(x−1). So you cannot simply cancel the x−1 in the denominator with the x−1 in the numerator. Lines 3 and 4 are the result of following this wrong expression.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.prompt: Fix Hyunwoo's solution by finding the left-hand limit and right-hand limit separately.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.hint.0: For x<1, cancel and simplify the expression, then find its value as x approaches 1. Use the same method for x>1.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the two values and check whether they meet the condition for a limit to exist.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you rewrite |x−1| separately for x<1 and for x>1?
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you conclude that there is no limit because the two limits differ?
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.model.0: If x>1, then |x−1|=x−1, so cancelling gives x+1, and the right-hand limit is 2. If x<1, then |x−1|=−(x−1), so it becomes −(x+1), and the left-hand limit is −2. The left-hand and right-hand limits differ, so the limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s2.model.1: The right-hand limit is x+1→2 for x greater than 1, and the left-hand limit is −(x+1)→−2 for x less than 1. The two values differ, so the limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.prompt: Choose the one of the following whose limit exists as x→1.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, first check whether the expression inside the absolute value changes sign near x=1.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether, if the sign does not change, you can simply remove the absolute value.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.r.a: This is the expression from the worked problem. The left-hand and right-hand limits differ.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.r.c: Near x=1, x+1 is positive, so |x²−1|=|x−1|(x+1), and the left-hand limit is −2 and the right-hand limit is 2, which differ.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.r.d: The numerator approaches 2 and the denominator approaches 0, so for x>1 it grows without bound and for x<1 it decreases without bound. The limit does not exist.
n-m-h2-limit-08.s.s3.explain: Near x=1, x+1>0, so |x+1|=x+1, and (x²−1)/|x+1|=x−1, so the limit is 0. What matters is whether the expression inside the absolute value changes sign near 1.

n-m-h2-limit-09.title: Inequalities and limits: examining Ayun's claim
n-m-h2-limit-09.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: order relations of limits
n-m-h2-limit-09.goal: Use a counterexample to see what happens to a strict inequality when you take limits, and explain whether the claim is true or false and what the correct conclusion is.
n-m-h2-limit-09.material: Ayun claims the following. "If f(x)<g(x) for every x(≠0) near x=0 and both limits lim f(x) and lim g(x) exist, then the limits also satisfy lim f(x) < lim g(x). The inequality stays the same."
n-m-h2-limit-09.thinking.0: Choosing the form of a counterexample
n-m-h2-limit-09.thinking.1: Explaining why the inequality gets weaker
n-m-h2-limit-09.prereq.1: Basic properties of limits of functions
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the pair (f, g) that works as a counterexample showing Ayun's claim is false. (as x→0)
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.hint.0: Split the claim into "assumption → conclusion," and remember that a counterexample satisfies the assumption but breaks the conclusion.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, check in turn whether f(x)<g(x) really holds for x≠0, and compare the sizes of the two limits.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.r.a: x²<0 does not hold for any x, so it does not satisfy the assumption of the claim.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.r.b: It satisfies the assumption and the limits satisfy −1<1, which agrees with Ayun's claim, so it is not a counterexample.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.r.d: x<x+1 holds and the limits satisfy 0<1, which agrees with Ayun's claim, so it is not a counterexample.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s1.explain: f(x)=0 and g(x)=x² satisfy f(x)<g(x) for x≠0, but both limits are equal to 0. It satisfies the assumption and fails the conclusion, so it is a counterexample.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.prompt: Write what happens in the limit to the inequality f(x)<g(x) as x gets close to 0. Also explain in one sentence, using a counterexample, why that happens.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.hint.0: Using the counterexample you chose in s1, write what happens to g(x)−f(x) as x gets close to 0.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what happens to the order relation of the two limits if that difference becomes arbitrarily small.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state in a sentence how the inequality changes?
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the f and g of your counterexample specifically?
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.model.0: In the limit, < weakens to ≤. If f(x)=0 and g(x)=x², then f<g for every x≠0, but the two limits are both 0. This is because the difference g−f gets arbitrarily close to 0.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s2.model.1: Taking limits can make them equal. For example, 0 is always less than x², but both have limit 0.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.prompt: When f(x)<g(x) for every x(≠0) near x=0 and both limits exist, choose the conclusion that is always true.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.hint.0: Check the order relation of the limits in both the counterexample from s1 and the example f=x, g=x+1.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.hint.1: Keep only the relation that is true in both examples.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.r.b: In the counterexample from s2, the limits were equal.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.r.c: Even though f<g, the limit of f cannot be the greater one.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.r.d: In the counterexample (0, x²), the two limits were equal.
n-m-h2-limit-09.s.s3.explain: If f(x)<g(x), only ≤ is guaranteed in the limit. There is an example where equality holds, so < is not true, and > is false in every case.

n-m-h2-limit-10.title: Checking a solution for finding a such that g(x)=f(x)f(x−a) is continuous
n-m-h2-limit-10.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: continuity of a product function
n-m-h2-limit-10.goal: Find and fix a solution that misses the special case where two discontinuity points coincide, and check why the function is continuous when they coincide.
n-m-h2-limit-10.material: For the function f(x)=x+2 (x<0), f(x)=x−2 (x≥0), the problem is to find all values of the constant a such that g(x)=f(x)f(x−a) is continuous at every real number x. Look at Eunwoo's solution.
n-m-h2-limit-10.thinking.0: Finding what the solution assumed without saying so
n-m-h2-limit-10.thinking.1: Checking the missing case by direct calculation
n-m-h2-limit-10.prereq.0: Left-hand and right-hand limits and continuity
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Eunwoo's solution.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, find what the solution takes for granted about the two points 0 and a.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.hint.1: Try special values of a and check whether the solution's claims still hold.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.line.0: f(x) is discontinuous only at x=0, and f(x−a) is discontinuous only at x=a.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.line.1: For g to be continuous at x=0, we need f(−a)=0, so a=2 or a=−2.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.line.2: For g to be continuous at x=a, we need f(a)=0, so a=2 or a=−2.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.line.3: So the values of a are −2 and 2.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first mistake. "For g to be continuous at x=0, we need f(−a)=0" is true only when f(x−a) is continuous near x=0. If a=0, then f(x−a)=f(x) is also discontinuous at x=0, so this statement does not hold. Line 3 makes the same assumption, and line 4 is the result.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.prompt: Find the value of a missing from Eunwoo's solution, and check that g is actually continuous at that value using the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value. At the end, write all values of a.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.hint.0: Break the assumption one piece at a time: write which a makes 0 and a the same point.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.hint.1: For that a, rewrite g as an expression, then find and compare its left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value at x=0.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write g as a specific expression when a=0?
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you find the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the function value?
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.model.0: If a=0, the two discontinuity points coincide at the single point x=0, and g(x)=f(x)·f(x). At x=0 the left-hand limit is 2²=4, the right-hand limit is (−2)²=4, and g(0)=4, so g is continuous. So the answer is a=−2, 0, 2.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s2.model.1: The solution assumed that the discontinuity points 0 and a are different points. If a=0, then g is the square of f(x), and the left-hand limit 4, right-hand limit 4, and function value 4 are equal, so g is continuous. Therefore a=−2, 0, 2.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.prompt: Choose the best reason why g(x)=f(x)f(x) is continuous at x=0 when a=0.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.hint.0: First write the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value of f at x=0.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate how these three values change when you square.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.o.a: Because the left-hand and right-hand limits of f differ only in sign, so they become equal when squared
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.r.a: You are right that they differ only in sign.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.o.b: Because the left-hand and right-hand limits of f are the same value
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.r.b: At x=0, f has left-hand limit 2 and right-hand limit −2, which differ.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.o.d: Because squaring any function always makes it continuous
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.r.d: There are functions that do not become continuous when squared. Example: left-hand limit 2, right-hand limit 3.
n-m-h2-limit-10.s.s3.explain: At x=0, the left-hand limit of f is 2, the right-hand limit is −2, and f(0)=−2. Squaring makes the left-hand limit 4, the right-hand limit 4, and the function value 4, all equal, so it is continuous. A discontinuity disappears under squaring only when the two sides differ merely in sign.

n-m-h2-limit-11.title: Is there the same time and the same spot? The mountain path problem
n-m-h2-limit-11.topic: Limits and continuity of functions: applying the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-11.goal: Define for yourself a new function that compares two situations, apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to show existence, and check the condition the theorem needs (continuity).
n-m-h2-limit-11.material: A person starts at the foot of a mountain at 8 a.m. and arrives at the summit at 6 p.m. along the same path. The next day the person starts at the summit at 8 a.m. and arrives at the foot of the mountain at 6 p.m. along the same path. On both days the person may rest or change speed along the way, but there is only one path. Let u(t) be the position on the first day at time t and d(t) the position on the second day, where position is the distance measured from the foot of the mountain (0 at the foot, D at the summit). Must there be a time at which the person is at the same spot on both days?
n-m-h2-limit-11.thinking.1: Writing an argument with the Intermediate Value Theorem
n-m-h2-limit-11.thinking.2: Checking the conclusion when a condition breaks
n-m-h2-limit-11.prereq.1: Experience of viewing position as a function of time
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.prompt: You want to turn "the same spot at the same time" into an equation and use the Intermediate Value Theorem. Which of the following is a suitable new function?
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write the event you want to find as the equation "u(t) equals d(t)."
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.hint.1: Find, among the options, a way to turn that equation into the form "some function = 0."
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.r.a: At t=8 and t=18 the value is D in both cases, so there is no sign change.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.r.c: h(t)=0 happens when one of the two is 0, which does not mean the two positions are equal.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.r.d: There are times when d(t)=0, so it is not defined, and when they are equal the value is just 1, not 0.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s1.explain: The same spot means u(t)=d(t), that is, u(t)−d(t)=0. If we set h(t)=u(t)−d(t), then h(8)=0−D<0 and h(18)=D−0>0, so the signs are opposite.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.prompt: Using h, write an explanation of why there must be a time at which the person is at the same spot on both days. Include the values of h at the two ends of the interval, the reason h can be regarded as continuous, and the theorem you use.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write the values of u and d at the starting time and the ending time, and find the values of h.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.hint.1: To use the theorem on h, say in words how the position must change over time.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the two endpoint values correctly?
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason for continuity to the story?
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.model.0: Let h(t)=u(t)−d(t). Then h(8)=0−D=−D<0 and h(18)=D−0=D>0. A person does not teleport, so the position changes without breaks, and u, d, and h are continuous. By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is c with h(c)=0, and then u(c)=d(c).
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s2.model.1: Setting h=u−d, it is the negative value −D at the start and the positive value D at the end. Position changes over time without breaks, so h is a continuous function, and by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is c between 8 and 18 with h(c)=0, so there is a time when the person is at the same spot at the same time.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.prompt: Suppose on the first day the person used a device that suddenly teleports them to the summit position at some moment (so the position changes with a break). Could we still say there must be a time at the same spot at the same time?
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine what the graph of h(t) looks like if the position jumps.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether, if the graph jumps, it can skip over 0 without passing through it even when the signs at the two ends are opposite.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.o.a: Yes: because opposite signs of h at the two ends are always enough
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.r.a: The signs alone are not enough. If continuity breaks, the theorem cannot be used.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.o.b: No: because on the day of teleporting, the person cannot reach the same spot
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.r.b: There is no basis for saying they cannot reach the same spot. They might still meet.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.o.c: It cannot be said that there must be one: because if continuity breaks, the Intermediate Value Theorem cannot be used
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.o.d: Yes: because the person walked for the same length of time on both days
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.r.d: The time taken being the same has no direct connection to the existence of a common spot.
n-m-h2-limit-11.s.s3.explain: For the theorem to guarantee it, h must be continuous. If the position jumps, h can skip over 0. For example, if on the first day the position jumps from 0 to D and on the second day it jumps from D to 0 at the same moment, the two positions might never be equal.

n-m-h2-seq-01.title: Checking Hayoon's solution for the common ratio
n-m-h2-seq-01.topic: Sum of a geometric sequence and finding the common ratio
n-m-h2-seq-01.goal: In a solution that uses the geometric sum formula, find the judgment that discards a solution, then correct it by writing the actual sequence with the discarded value and checking the condition.
n-m-h2-seq-01.material: This is Hayoon's solution for finding the common ratio of a geometric sequence {aₙ} with first term 2 whose sum from the first term to the third term is 6. (aₙ is "a sub n," r is the common ratio, and S₃ is the sum of the first 3 terms.)
n-m-h2-seq-01.thinking.0: Checking what assumption each line was written on
n-m-h2-seq-01.thinking.1: Checking by putting the discarded value directly into the condition
n-m-h2-seq-01.thinking.2: Splitting into cases before using the formula
n-m-h2-seq-01.prereq.0: The general term of a geometric sequence and the formula for the sum of the first n terms
n-m-h2-seq-01.prereq.1: Solving a quadratic equation by factoring
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Hayoon's solution that contains a wrong judgment. (If more than one line is wrong, choosing any of them is fine.)
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, check whether the expression can be used for every r or becomes meaningless for some r.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each value of r that appears in the solution, write out the sequence with that common ratio and test whether the sum of its first 3 terms is 6.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.line.0: Let the common ratio be r. By the geometric sum formula, S₃ = 2(r³−1)/(r−1) = 6.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.line.1: Since (r³−1)/(r−1) = r²+r+1, we get r²+r+1 = 3, that is, r²+r−2 = 0.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.line.3: But if r = 1, the denominator r−1 is 0 and the expression does not hold, so we discard r = 1. Therefore the common ratio is only −2.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s1.explain: If the common ratio is 1, the sum formula a(rⁿ−1)/(r−1) cannot be used. The first line used the formula without treating that case separately, and the last line discarded r=1 for the reason that "it cannot be put into the formula." But if r=1, the sequence is 2, 2, 2, … and the sum of the first 3 terms is 6, so it satisfies the condition. So the common ratio is −2 or 1.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.prompt: Show why discarding r=1 is wrong by writing out the sequence for r=1, and write all the correct common ratios.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write out the first three terms of the sequence whose common ratio is the discarded value of r.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.hint.1: Add those three terms and compare with the sum in the condition, then think about which case should have been examined separately before using the formula.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: if the common ratio is 1, the sequence is ..., so ...
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write out the sequence for common ratio 1?
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish between a value that cannot be put into the formula and a value that cannot exist as a sequence?
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.model.0: If r=1, the sequence is 2, 2, 2, … and the sum of the first 3 terms is 6. It satisfies the condition, so it must not be discarded. So the common ratio is −2 or 1.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.model.1: The denominator being 0 only means the formula cannot be used; a sequence with common ratio 1 exists. 2+2+2=6, so r=1 is also a solution. The answer is r=−2 and r=1.
n-m-h2-seq-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It means the same if you explain that r=1 was handled separately without using the formula.

n-m-h2-seq-02.title: If the induction step is correct, is the statement correct too?
n-m-h2-seq-02.topic: Logic of mathematical induction: the induction step and the base step
n-m-h2-seq-02.goal: Understand, while revising your judgment as information is revealed, that in mathematical induction the "induction step" is only a conditional statement and that the conclusion stands only if the starting case is verified.
n-m-h2-seq-02.material: Jia wants to show by induction that "P(n): 2+4+6+⋯+2n = n²+n+3" holds for every natural number n. What she checked is revealed one piece at a time.
n-m-h2-seq-02.thinking.0: Revising the judgment each time new information appears
n-m-h2-seq-02.thinking.1: Understanding the meaning of the conditional "if ..., then the next ... too"
n-m-h2-seq-02.thinking.2: Telling apart what each of the two checks in induction does
n-m-h2-seq-02.prereq.0: Sum of an arithmetic sequence and the Σ symbol
n-m-h2-seq-02.prereq.1: The form of mathematical induction (checking the first case and the step from k to k+1)
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose a judgment using only the information revealed.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, consider whether your judgment should change.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether "if P(k), then P(k+1)" can be true even when P(k) is false.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.info: The induction step has been checked. Assume P(k) holds and add 2(k+1) to both sides; the right side becomes k²+k+3+2(k+1) = (k+1)²+(k+1)+3, so for every natural number k, "if P(k) holds, then P(k+1) holds" is correct.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this information alone, can we say that "P(n) holds for every natural number n"?
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.after: The induction step is the conditional statement "if P(k), then P(k+1)." P must actually hold somewhere for it to carry on from there.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We can say so: because the step from k to the next has been checked for every k
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The induction step was written on the assumption "if it holds," so you need a case where it actually holds somewhere.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We cannot decide yet: because the first case where it holds has not been checked
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You thought about the fact that a separate check of the starting case is needed.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We cannot say so, and the statement is false: because having only the induction step makes it false
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The step being correct and the statement being false are different matters. There is not yet any evidence that it is false.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Now the starting case has been checked. For n=1, the left side is 2 and the right side is 1+1+3 = 5.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: With this information added, what is your judgment?
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.after: If P(1) is false, the path from 1 on to 2, 3, … is blocked from the start. Even if the induction step is correct, it does not follow that P(2) is true.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Only P(1) is false: from n=2 on, the induction step keeps carrying it on, so it holds
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If P(1) is false, the induction step gives no basis for P(2) being true.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The induction step is wrong, so it must be checked again
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The calculation in the induction step was correct. What is false is P(1).
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The path that starts from P(1) and carries on is blocked: the induction step alone cannot prove this statement
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought about the fact that, because P(1) is false, "if P(1) then P(2)" has nothing to carry on from.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.info: I calculated n=2, 3, 4 directly. The left sides are 6, 12, 20 and the right sides are 9, 15, 23. In fact 2+4+⋯+2n = n²+n, so the right side is always 3 larger.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What does this result tell us about the induction step?
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.after: "If P(k), then P(k+1)" is true for every k, but P(n) is false for every n. Even if a conditional statement is true, if the hypothesis is always false, the conclusion does not follow.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Even if the induction step is correct, the statement can be false for every n if the start is false
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You distinguished "if P(k), then P(k+1)" being correct from P actually holding.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The induction step was correct, so the statement holds for at least some n
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The step being correct does not guarantee that even one n satisfies the statement.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The statement became false because the calculation in the induction step was wrong
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The calculation in the induction step was correct. A correct step and a false statement can exist together.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked as if checking the induction step alone would be enough, but when the starting case was checked, the path was blocked. In induction, you need both "the start is true" and "if it is true, the next is also true."
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.prompt: Write the two things you must check to show "it holds for every natural number n" by induction, and explain in one or two sentences which of them fell apart in Jia's case.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.hint.0: Thinking of induction as a chain of dominoes, write separately what knocking down the first domino and carrying on each correspond to.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.hint.1: Look again at the result of the one Jia checked that corresponds to the first domino.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say what each of the two checks guarantees?
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you point out which one is missing or wrong in Jia's solution?
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.model.0: First, you must check whether the statement holds when n=1. Second, you must show that if P(k) holds, then P(k+1) holds. Jia got the second right, but at n=1 we have 2≠5, so the first is false.
n-m-h2-seq-02.s.s2.model.1: You need to look at two things: whether the starting case (P(1)) is true, and whether the step from k to k+1 works. For Jia, P(1) does not hold, so the start falls apart.

n-m-h2-seq-03.title: The proof that 2ⁿ is greater than n²: where is the problem?
n-m-h2-seq-03.topic: Mathematical induction: the range of k for which the induction step holds
n-m-h2-seq-03.goal: Check whether the inequality used in the induction step holds for every k, and reset the starting case to match the range where the step holds.
n-m-h2-seq-03.material: Seoyun proved by mathematical induction that "2ⁿ > n² for every natural number n." (2ⁿ is 2 to the n-th power, and 2ᵏ⁺¹ is 2 to the (k+1)-th power.)
n-m-h2-seq-03.thinking.0: Testing the inequality in the induction step with specific values of k
n-m-h2-seq-03.thinking.1: Checking the statement itself for small n
n-m-h2-seq-03.thinking.2: Moving the starting case to match the range where the step holds
n-m-h2-seq-03.prereq.1: Properties of inequalities and expanding expressions
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Seoyun's proof.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.hint.0: In the equation or inequality each line claims, put 1, 2, 3, … in the place of k and check whether it actually holds.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.hint.1: Test with small n whether the conclusion of the proof is really correct, and if it is false, trace back to find which line made that possible.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.line.0: P(n): 2ⁿ > n². For n=1, 2 > 1, so P(1) holds.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.line.4: Therefore 2ᵏ⁺¹ > (k+1)², that is, P(k+1) also holds. By induction, 2ⁿ > n² for every natural number n.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the first mistake. k²−2k−1 ≥ 0 does not hold for every natural number k. If k=1 it is −2, and if k=2 it is −1. It holds from natural numbers 3 and up. The conclusion in line 5 follows from line 4. In fact, 2ⁿ > n² does not hold for n=2, 3, 4.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.prompt: To fix this into a correct proof, determine the range of n for which 2ⁿ>n² holds, write which case should be checked as the starting case, and what condition on k the induction step can use.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate 2ⁿ and n² for n=1 to 6, make a table, and find the first n from which 2ⁿ stays greater.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find the k from which the inequality in the wrong line starts to hold, and think about whether you can set the starting case at or above that k.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: it holds when n is at least ..., and ...
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say that even if it holds at n=1, the argument does not carry on if the step fails at k=1, 2?
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you choose the starting case within the range where the step works?
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.model.0: 2ⁿ>n² holds from n=5. Start with n=5, where 32>25, and the step's inequality k²−2k−1≥0 holds for k≥3, so the step can be used for k≥5.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.model.1: It holds for n≥5. Check the start at n=5 (32>25), and since 2k²≥(k+1)² is true when k is at least 3, it carries on for every k≥5.
n-m-h2-seq-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: For an answer that gives the range as n at least 3 rather than starting at n=5, check whether it has verified that the statement is actually false at n=3, 4.

n-m-h2-seq-04.title: Is a₄ 6, or could it be −6 too?
n-m-h2-seq-04.topic: The geometric mean term of a geometric sequence and its sign
n-m-h2-seq-04.goal: From the two candidates that come from the geometric mean relation a₄²=a₂a₆, judge whether the structure of a geometric sequence determines the sign, and explain the reason by comparing with the case of three consecutive terms.
n-m-h2-seq-04.material: In a geometric sequence {aₙ} of real numbers, a₂=3 and a₆=12. Minjun said, "a₄²=a₂×a₆=36, so a₄=6 or −6," and Seoyeon said, "a₄ is only 6." (aₙ is "a sub n," and the common ratio is the ratio of two adjacent terms.)
n-m-h2-seq-04.thinking.0: Filtering the candidates from the squared relation by the structure
n-m-h2-seq-04.thinking.1: Expressing terms with the first term and common ratio to check the sign
n-m-h2-seq-04.thinking.2: Comparing two cases with different conditions
n-m-h2-seq-04.prereq.0: The general term of a geometric sequence aₙ=arⁿ⁻¹
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct judgment among the two people's statements, along with its reason.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.hint.0: Express a₄ and a₆ in terms of a₂ and the common ratio r.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.hint.1: In the expressions you wrote, compare whether r is multiplied an odd number of times or an even number of times.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.o.a: a₄ = 6 or −6: because both numbers with a₄²=36 are geometric means
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.r.a: You accepted both values by looking only at the squared relation. You did not check whether they are possible in an actual sequence.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be determined: because without knowing the common ratio r, a₄ cannot be known either
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.r.b: Even if r is not determined, check whether r² is determined.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.o.c: a₄ = 6 only: because a geometric sequence cannot have a negative term
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.r.c: If the common ratio is negative, negative terms appear. In this case the reason the sign is determined lies elsewhere.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.o.d: a₄ = 6 only: because a₄=a₂×r² and r²≥0, so a₄ has the same sign as a₂
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.r.d: This is the thought of writing the term in terms of a₂ and the common ratio to check the sign.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s1.explain: a₄=a₂×r² and r² is at least 0, so a₄ has the same sign as a₂=3. Also, from a₆=a₂×r⁴ we get r⁴=4, so r²=2 and a₄=6. The common ratio r=±√2 are both possible, but a₄ is the same value. Looking only at a₄²=36 would give −6 as well, but it is impossible in the actual sequence.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.prompt: If 3, x, 12 are three consecutive terms of a geometric sequence, both x=6 and x=−6 are possible. But when a₂=3 and a₆=12, a₄ can only be 6. Explain why the two cases are different.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.hint.0: In each case, count how many times the common ratio is multiplied to the preceding term to get the middle term.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare what the sign of that product is when the common ratio is negative.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: for three consecutive terms ..., but a₄ ...
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write x=3r and a₄=3r² respectively?
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say what happens in the two cases when r is negative?
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.model.0: For three consecutive terms, x=3r, so the common ratio can be 2 or −2 and x can be 6 or −6. But multiplying by r twice, as in a₄=a₂r², removes the sign of the common ratio, so it always has the same sign as 3.
n-m-h2-seq-04.s.s2.model.1: If the middle term is x=3r, then x is negative when r is negative. a₄ is a₂ times r², so it is positive whether r is positive or negative. So a₄ can only be 6.

n-m-h2-seq-05.title: Three numbers that form an arithmetic sequence and, after reordering, a geometric sequence
n-m-h2-seq-05.topic: The structure formed by arithmetic and geometric sequences together
n-m-h2-seq-05.goal: Build examples of three numbers forming an arithmetic sequence that become a geometric sequence when reordered, and find the common structure among the examples.
n-m-h2-seq-05.material: There are three distinct nonzero integers x, y, z. You want x, y, z to form an arithmetic sequence in this order, and to form a geometric sequence when the order of the three numbers is changed.
n-m-h2-seq-05.thinking.0: Building an example that satisfies both conditions at once
n-m-h2-seq-05.thinking.1: Finding the constraint that arises when both conditions overlap in the same order
n-m-h2-seq-05.thinking.2: Finding a pattern in several examples
n-m-h2-seq-05.prereq.0: Arithmetic mean term and geometric mean term
n-m-h2-seq-05.prereq.1: Finding and testing numbers that satisfy an equation within the integers
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.prompt: When do three numbers x, y, z form an arithmetic sequence "in this order" and also a geometric sequence "in the same order"? (Consider only nonzero numbers.)
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write that both the arithmetic condition 2y=x+z and the geometric condition y²=xz hold, and eliminate y.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.hint.1: Look at the relationship between x and z in the resulting equation.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.o.a: When the common difference and common ratio are equal
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.r.a: The common difference and common ratio mean different things, so being equal does not guarantee that both conditions hold together.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.o.b: Whenever y is between x and z
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.r.b: Being the arithmetic mean term and being the geometric mean term are different conditions.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.o.c: Only when all three numbers are the same
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.r.c: For an arithmetic sequence, 2y=x+z, and for a geometric sequence in the same order, y²=xz. Check what happens when you use both together.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.o.d: Whenever the common difference is not 0
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.r.d: Pick one example with a nonzero common difference and check the geometric condition.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s1.explain: From 2y=x+z and y²=xz, xz=((x+z)/2)², so (x−z)²=0, that is, x=z. Then all three numbers are the same. If the three numbers are distinct, the two conditions cannot hold together in the same order, so the order must be changed.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.prompt: Enter two or more different examples in which x, y, z form an arithmetic sequence in this order and form a geometric sequence when the order of the three numbers is suitably changed. (x, y, z are distinct nonzero integers with absolute value at most 100.)
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.hint.0: Split into cases according to which of the three numbers, y, x, or z, can be the middle term of the geometric sequence. What you found in the first step lets you eliminate one of them.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.hint.1: Once the middle term is fixed, solve the geometric mean equation together with y−x=z−y to find the ratio of the three numbers, and choose integers that fit that ratio.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.ok.c1: Nonzero integers with absolute value at most 100.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.fail.c1: x, y, z must be nonzero integers with absolute value at most 100.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The three numbers must be distinct.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.ok.c3: x, y, z form an arithmetic sequence in this order.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.fail.c3: y−x and z−y are not equal.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.ok.c4: They form a geometric sequence when reordered.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.fail.c4: They do not form a geometric sequence in any order.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.explain: (−2, 1, 4) has common difference 3, and arranged as 1, −2, 4 it is a geometric sequence with common ratio −2. Every example in this range is an integer multiple of (−2, 1, 4) or its reverse order. By the result of the first step, that three distinct numbers cannot form an arithmetic sequence and a geometric sequence in the same order, the middle term of the reordered geometric sequence is either x or z.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write the pattern you found by comparing the examples.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Divide the three numbers of each example by their greatest common factor to get the smallest integer ratio, and compare.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether both conditions still hold when you multiply one example by any integer.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: the examples I found are all ...
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the same pattern applies to all the examples?
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you try making a new example with the pattern?
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.model.0: All the examples I found are multiples of −2, 1, 4, or the reverse of that. The ratio of the three numbers is the same, −2:1:4.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.model.1: They were (−2, 1, 4) multiplied by numbers such as 2, 3, −5. There was also an example with the order changed to 4, 1, −2.
n-m-h2-seq-05.s.s2.because.model.2: With the middle number y as the reference, x and z were −2 times and 4 times y.

n-m-h2-seq-06.title: Can this information determine the sum of the first 10 terms?
n-m-h2-seq-06.topic: Sums of arithmetic sequences and the information needed
n-m-h2-seq-06.goal: Distinguish information that is sufficient from information that is insufficient to determine the sum of the first 10 terms of an arithmetic sequence, show the insufficient cases with counterexamples, and find what the sufficient information has in common.
n-m-h2-seq-06.material: You want to determine the sum S₁₀=a₁+a₂+⋯+a₁₀ from the first term through the 10th term of an arithmetic sequence {aₙ} as a single value. (The first term and common difference are unknown.) Consider the case where each piece of information below is given alone.
n-m-h2-seq-06.thinking.1: Showing that information is insufficient using two different sequences
n-m-h2-seq-06.thinking.2: Finding the common structure of the sufficient pieces of information
n-m-h2-seq-06.prereq.0: The general term of an arithmetic sequence
n-m-h2-seq-06.prereq.1: The formula for the sum of an arithmetic sequence
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information for which that one piece alone determines the value of S₁₀ as a single value.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.hint.0: Pair up S₁₀ as the first and last terms, the second and second-to-last terms, and so on. Look at the sum of the indices in each pair.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, check whether the sum of its indices equals the sum of the indices of such a pair.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.r.a: Check whether the sum of the indices of the two terms (10) equals the sum of the indices of the first term and the 10th term.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.r.b: You thought about the fact that the sum of the indices of the two terms equals the sum of the indices when pairing up in S₁₀.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.r.c: With only one term, the common difference is not determined, so check whether the sum is determined.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.r.d: This is the choice made by checking whether the sum of the indices equals that of the pairs of S₁₀.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.r.e: Check whether the sum of the indices of the two terms (12) equals the sum of the indices when pairing.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s1.explain: If you group S₁₀ into five pairs a₁+a₁₀, a₂+a₉, …, the sum of the indices in each pair is 11 and the sums of the pairs are all equal. So if the sum of two terms whose indices add to 11 is given, S₁₀=5×(that sum)=90 is determined. a₃+a₇, a₅, and a₄+a₈ are not such pairs, so they do not determine it.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to show that a₃+a₇=18 alone does not determine S₁₀. Enter two arithmetic sequences, as (first term a, common difference d), that satisfy a₃+a₇=18 but have different values of S₁₀.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write a₃ and a₇ in terms of a and d, and from a₃+a₇=18 express a in terms of d.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change d and find a each time, then calculate S₁₀=10a+45d for each and compare.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.fail.c1: a₃+a₇ is not 18. a₃=a+2d and a₇=a+6d.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.explain: If a₃+a₇=2a+8d=18, then a=9−4d. S₁₀=10a+45d=90+5d, so it depends on the common difference d. For example, (9, 0) gives 90, (5, 1) gives 95, and (1, 2) gives 100.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Write the criterion that separates the sufficient pieces of information (a₂+a₉, a₄+a₇) from the insufficient ones (a₃+a₇, a₄+a₈).
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: When you group S₁₀ into pairs, write the indices of the two terms in a pair and compare the sums of their indices.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: In the insufficient pieces of information, check what you get when you add the indices of the two terms.
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: if the sum of the indices is ..., then ...
n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use whether the sum of the indices is 11 as your criterion?
