n-m-h2-seq-06.s.s2.because.model.1: Only two terms whose indices add to 11 (the same total as when pairing the first and last terms) determine S₁₀. Index sums of 10 or 12 do not match up as pairs.

n-m-h2-seq-07.title: Why does subtracting 3 give a geometric sequence?
n-m-h2-seq-07.topic: Solving and explaining the recurrence aₙ₊₁=paₙ+q
n-m-h2-seq-07.goal: Understand why, in solving a recurrence, subtracting the unchanging value turns it into a geometric sequence, and explain it again to a middle-school friend so that the reason shows.
n-m-h2-seq-07.material:
A lab is growing bacteria. At first there are 5, and every hour the number doubles and then 3 are removed. For the number aₙ at hour n (with a₁=5 for the first hour), aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ − 3. Below is a senior student's solution note.
Note: From x = 2x − 3, x = 3. So aₙ₊₁ − 3 = 2(aₙ − 3). Let bₙ = aₙ − 3. Then b₁ = 2 and bₙ = 2ⁿ. Therefore aₙ = 2ⁿ + 3.
n-m-h2-seq-07.thinking.0: Figuring out what each line of the solution does
n-m-h2-seq-07.thinking.1: Rewriting a solution that lacks reasons so that the reasons show
n-m-h2-seq-07.thinking.2: Writing an explanation suited to the listener's level
n-m-h2-seq-07.prereq.0: The general term of a geometric sequence
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.prompt: What is "x = 2x − 3, so x = 3" in the note looking for?
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put 3 in place of aₙ in the recurrence and calculate what aₙ₊₁ becomes.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that result with what you get when you put in another value (for example, 5).
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.o.a: Checking that the first term is 3
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.r.a: a₁ is given as 5. Look again at where the 3 came from.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.o.b: Finding the general term of the sequence right away
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.r.b: x=3 is just a single number, not an expression that depends on n.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.o.c: Finding a value that stays the same even after one hour
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.r.c: You thought about the fact that if aₙ=3 then aₙ₊₁=2·3−3=3, so it is a value that does not change.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.o.d: Finding that the common ratio is 3
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.r.d: The common ratio is 2. Check that 3 is not the common ratio.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s1.explain: The solution x=3 of x=2x−3 is a number that does not change when put into the recurrence, because if aₙ=3 then aₙ₊₁=3. Subtracting this value removes the unchanging part, leaving only "doubling," so it becomes a geometric sequence.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the note as if explaining it to a middle-school friend. It must show what kind of number "3" is and why subtracting 3 from aₙ makes the problem easier.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate how many bacteria there will be after one hour if the number is 3, and put it in your story.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write in one sentence how the new sequence, with 3 subtracted, changes each hour.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: First, find the number that ... Subtract that number and ...
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain without using words your friend does not know (terms like fixed point)?
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is "why subtract 3" clearer than in the note?
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.model.0: First, find the number of bacteria that does not change after one hour. Solving 2x−3=x gives x=3. When there are 3, they double to 6, and removing 3 leaves 3 again. Now subtract 3 from the number at each hour. Then what is left exactly doubles every hour, so it is a geometric sequence that doubles each time.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.model.1: If there are 3 bacteria, doubling and then removing leaves 3 again. So 3 is a reference that does not change. If you make bₙ by subtracting 3 from aₙ, then bₙ₊₁ is twice bₙ. A sequence that doubles each time, starting at 2, becomes 2ⁿ, so aₙ=2ⁿ+3.
n-m-h2-seq-07.s.s2.model.2: 3 is the number that stays in place when you double and then reduce. If you subtract it, what remains keeps doubling.

n-m-h2-seq-08.title: Making a sequence whose first term to exceed 810 is the 6th term
n-m-h2-seq-08.topic: The first term of a geometric sequence to exceed a benchmark
n-m-h2-seq-08.goal: Translate the condition "the first term to exceed" into inequalities, decide how to handle the equal case at the boundary, and build a geometric sequence that satisfies the condition yourself.
n-m-h2-seq-08.material: In a geometric sequence {aₙ} with first term a and common ratio r, a and r are natural numbers and r is at least 2. You want to build the sequence so that, among its terms, the first to exceed 810 (to become greater than 810) is the 6th term.
n-m-h2-seq-08.thinking.0: Translating a condition in words into inequalities
n-m-h2-seq-08.thinking.1: Deciding how to handle the boundary value (the equal case)
n-m-h2-seq-08.thinking.2: Verifying your own example by calculation
n-m-h2-seq-08.prereq.0: The general term of a geometric sequence
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct way to write the condition "the first term to exceed 810 is the 6th term" as an expression.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the 5th term and the 6th term in terms of a and r.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether "exceed" includes "equal," and so which inequality sign the 5th term needs.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.r.a: This expresses that the 5th term does not exceed it (equality included) and the 6th term exceeds it for the first time.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.r.b: It only wrote that the 6th term is greater than 810. It does not rule out the case where it was already exceeded before the 5th term.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.r.c: It left out the case where the 5th term equals 810. If the 5th term is 810, consider whether it has "exceeded" 810.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.r.d: It shifted the term number by one. Check what power of r multiplies a in the 6th term.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s1.explain: The 6th term is a×r⁵ and the 5th term is a×r⁴. The terms keep growing, so up to the 5th term they must not exceed 810 (equal does not count as exceeding, so at most 810), and the 6th term must be greater than 810. That is, a×r⁴ ≤ 810 < a×r⁵.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.prompt: Enter three different pairs (a, r) that satisfy the condition. (a is a natural number from 1 to 100 and r is a natural number from 2 to 20.)
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a common ratio first, then change a and calculate the 5th and 6th terms and compare them with 810.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.hint.1: If you go out of range, decrease or increase a so that 810 lies between the 5th and 6th terms.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a and r are natural numbers within the range.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be a natural number from 1 to 100 and r a natural number from 2 to 20.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The 5th term is greater than 810, so 810 was already exceeded before that.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The 6th term is not greater than 810.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.explain: For (10, 3), the 5th term is 810 and the 6th term is 2430. If the 5th term is exactly 810, it has not exceeded 810, so this example also satisfies the condition. For (3, 3), the 6th term is 729, so it has not yet exceeded 810, and for (20, 3), the 5th term is 1620, so it has already exceeded it.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of your examples, calculate the 5th and 6th terms and compare them with 810, and decide and write whether the case where the 5th term is exactly 810 also satisfies the condition.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the result of calculating the 5th and 6th terms for your chosen (a, r) and comparing their sizes with 810.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find a sequence whose 5th term equals 810 and work out which term is the first to exceed 810 in that sequence.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: if (a, r)=(...), the 5th term is ... and the 6th term is ...
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write "greater" or "less" when comparing the calculated values with 810?
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you base your judgment on "equal does not count as exceeding"?
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.model.0: For (10, 3), the 5th term is 10×81=810 and the 6th term is 2430. If the 5th term is 810, it has not exceeded 810, so the 6th term is the first to exceed it, and the condition is met.
n-m-h2-seq-08.s.s2.because.model.1: With (2, 4), the 5th term is 512 and the 6th term is 2048, so 512 ≤ 810 < 2048. In the case where the 5th term is exactly 810 it is also not greater than 810, so the first term to exceed it is the 6th term, which is fine.

n-m-h2-seq-09.title: If the sum keeps growing, do the terms keep growing too?
n-m-h2-seq-09.topic: The sum Sₙ of a sequence and the increase or decrease of the term aₙ
n-m-h2-seq-09.goal: Build counterexamples yourself to confirm that Sₙ increasing is different from aₙ increasing, and explain the increase or decrease of Sₙ using the signs of the terms.
n-m-h2-seq-09.material: The first term a and common difference d of an arithmetic sequence {aₙ} are integers, and Sₙ=a₁+a₂+⋯+aₙ. Mina said, "If the sum keeps growing, as in S₁<S₂<⋯<S₆, then the sequence {aₙ} also keeps growing."
n-m-h2-seq-09.thinking.0: Building a counterexample to the claim
n-m-h2-seq-09.thinking.1: Seeing with an expression what the increase in the sum is
n-m-h2-seq-09.thinking.2: Translating the condition into inequalities and finding an example
n-m-h2-seq-09.prereq.0: The general term and sum of an arithmetic sequence
n-m-h2-seq-09.prereq.1: The relationship between Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁ and aₙ
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.prompt: What exactly does the statement S₁<S₂<S₃<S₄<S₅<S₆ tell us about {aₙ}?
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.hint.0: Express the difference of Sₖ₊₁ and Sₖ using aₖ₊₁.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write what must be positive for that difference to be positive.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.o.a: a₁<a₂<⋯<a₆, that is, the terms also keep growing
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.r.a: This treats the sum growing and the terms growing as the same. To check whether the two increases are the same, find Sₖ₊₁−Sₖ.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.r.b: The sum being positive alone does not tell you whether the sum decreased somewhere in the middle.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.o.c: The common difference d is positive
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.r.c: Even if d is not positive, the sum grows as long as the terms are positive.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.o.d: a₂, a₃, …, a₆ are all positive
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.r.d: This is the thought of using the relation Sₖ₊₁−Sₖ=aₖ₊₁.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s1.explain: Sₖ₊₁ = Sₖ + aₖ₊₁, so Sₖ<Sₖ₊₁ is the same as aₖ₊₁>0. Therefore S₁<S₂<⋯<S₆ means a₂ through a₆ are all positive. Even if the terms get smaller (even if the common difference is negative), the sum keeps growing as long as they are positive.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.prompt: Enter two or more different arithmetic sequences, as (first term a, common difference d), that show Mina's statement is wrong. There are three conditions. The terms decrease (d<0), S₁<S₂<⋯<S₆ holds, and from some point the sum actually decreases, so that S₁₂<S₁₁. (a and d are integers)
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether, for a₂ through a₆ to be all positive, it is enough that the smallest, a₆=a+5d, is positive.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one d and determine the range of a with two inequalities.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.fail.c1: a and d must be integers.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The common difference is negative, so the terms decrease.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The terms must decrease, so d must be negative.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.ok.c3: a₂ through a₆ are positive, so S₁<⋯<S₆.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.fail.c3: a₂, a₃, …, a₆ are not all positive. Check up to a₆=a+5d.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.fail.c4: a₁₂ is not negative, so S₁₂<S₁₁ does not hold.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.explain: For (6, −1) the terms are 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, … and S₁ through S₆ keep growing, but a₁₂=−5<0, so S₁₂<S₁₁. For (3, −1), a₆=−2, so S₆<S₅, and for (20, −1), a₁₂=9 is positive, so S₁₂ is also greater than S₁₁.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.prompt: For the sequence you found, explain why the sum first grows and then decreases, using the relation between the change in the sum and the terms.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write S₇ in terms of S₆ and a₇.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write whether S₇ becomes greater or less than S₆ when a₇ is positive and when it is negative.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: the sum grows or decreases because ...
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish that the sum grows if the term is positive and decreases if it is negative?
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The sum changes each time by adding a new term. If that term is positive, the sum grows, and if it is negative, the sum decreases. Even if the terms get smaller, the sum keeps growing as long as they are positive, and once a term becomes negative, the sum decreases.
n-m-h2-seq-09.s.s2.because.model.1: Since Sₖ₊₁=Sₖ+aₖ₊₁, the sum grows if the added term aₖ₊₁ is positive and shrinks if it is negative. The common difference is negative, so at some point a term becomes negative and the sum decreases.

n-m-h2-seq-10.title: Does the sum of differences run to n or to n−1?
n-m-h2-seq-10.topic: The general term of a difference sequence and the range of the sum
n-m-h2-seq-10.goal: Test two candidates for the general term obtained from the recurrence with small values of n to sort them out, and explain with concrete terms why the sum of differences goes up to n−1.
n-m-h2-seq-10.material:
Two students each found the general term of the sequence {aₙ} with a₁=2 and aₙ₊₁ = aₙ + (3n − 1).
Harin: aₙ = 2 + Σ(k=1 to n−1)(3k−1) = (3n²−5n+6)/2
Doyun: aₙ = 2 + Σ(k=1 to n)(3k−1) = (3n²+n+4)/2
n-m-h2-seq-10.thinking.0: Calculating the candidates directly at small n and comparing them
n-m-h2-seq-10.thinking.1: Counting the number of terms in the sum
n-m-h2-seq-10.thinking.2: Judging based on the results of the check
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.prompt: If you find a₂ and a₃ from the recurrence and put n=1, 2, 3 into the two expressions and compare, what result do you get?
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.hint.0: First calculate a₂ and a₃ directly from the recurrence and write them in a table.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare those values one by one with the values of the two expressions at n=1, 2, 3.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.o.a: Both expressions equal a₂ at n=2, so both are possible
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.r.a: Put n=2 into Doyun's expression and calculate whether it equals a₂.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.o.b: Harin's expression gets all three values right and Doyun's gets all three wrong
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.r.b: This describes the result of calculating the three values directly from the recurrence and comparing.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.o.c: Doyun's expression is wrong only at n=1 and right at n=2, 3
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.r.c: Calculate at n=2, 3 as well and compare with the values found from the recurrence.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.o.d: Doyun's expression is just shifted by one place and is the same expression, so either can be used
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.r.d: What matters is whether the two expressions give the same value when the same n is put in. A shifted expression is not the same expression.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s1.explain: By the recurrence, a₁=2, a₂=2+2=4, a₃=4+5=9. Harin's expression gives 2, 4, 9, all correct. Doyun's expression gives 4, 9, 17, all three wrong. The value Doyun's expression gives for n is actually aₙ₊₁, because ending the sum at n adds one more term.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.prompt: Using a₄ as an example, explain why the sum of differences must run from k=1 to n−1. (Count how many additions starting from a₁ it takes to make a₄.)
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.hint.0: In turn, write how many differences are added to a₁ to make a₂, a₃, and a₄.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare that count with the term number and write the pattern in one sentence.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.placeholder: Example: a₄ is made by adding ... times to a₁, so ...
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you count how many additions from the first term a₁ it takes to get aₙ?
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you think about the fact that the sum is empty when n=1?
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.model.0: a₂ is made by adding one difference to a₁, a₃ by adding two, and a₄ by adding three (2, 5, 8). a₄=2+15=17. So aₙ is a₁ plus n−1 differences, and the sum must go up to k=n−1.
n-m-h2-seq-10.s.s2.model.1: a₄ is the value obtained by starting from a₁=2 and adding the three differences 2, 5, 8. That is, you add one fewer terms than the term number, so aₙ is the sum from k=1 to n−1.

n-m-h2-trig-01.title: Checking a solution that found how far a graph was moved
n-m-h2-trig-01.goal: In a solution that finds how far the graph of the form y=a sin(bx−c) has been shifted from the graph of y=a sin bx, find and fix the wrong line, and check the corrected value directly.
n-m-h2-trig-01.material: Jiyun solved how the graph of y=2sin(3x−π/2) is a shift of the graph of y=2sin3x, as below. (π is pi and angles are in radians. 2sin3x means 2 times sine of 3x.)
n-m-h2-trig-01.thinking.0: Following the solution line by line to find the wrong line
n-m-h2-trig-01.thinking.1: Factoring out the coefficient of x to read the translation
n-m-h2-trig-01.thinking.2: Expanding the corrected expression to check
n-m-h2-trig-01.prereq.0: The period and maximum and minimum of y=a sin bx
n-m-h2-trig-01.prereq.1: Translating a graph in the x-direction means replacing x with x−m
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Jiyun's solution.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check line by line whether each line really follows from the line just before it.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.hint.1: Expand the factored expression again by the distributive law and compare it with the expression before factoring.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.line.1: The maximum is 2 and the minimum is −2.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.line.3: Therefore this graph is the graph of y=2sin3x translated by π/2 in the x-direction.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s1.explain: The 3rd line is wrong. Expanding 3(x−π/2) gives 3x−3π/2, which differs from 3x−π/2. Since 3x−π/2=3(x−π/6), the shift is π/6. The 4th line is a conclusion following the wrong result of the 3rd line, and the 1st and 2nd lines are correct.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.prompt: Fix the wrong line and write the correct direction and amount of the shift, together with one way you checked that the value is right.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.hint.0: Starting from 3x−π/2, think about what number must come in front of the parentheses to form x−(shift).
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.hint.1: Expand the expression written with the shift you found and check that it becomes 3x−π/2.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: if you factor 3x−π/2 as ..., you get ...
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you expand the corrected expression yourself?
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you say why it must be factored by 3?
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also state the direction of the shift (to the right)?
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.model.0: In 3x−π/2, first factor out 3 to get 3(x−π/6). So y=2sin3x was shifted to the right by π/6. Check: expanding 3(x−π/6) gives 3x−π/2, the same as the original expression.
n-m-h2-trig-01.s.s2.model.1: You must factor out the coefficient 3 of x to get the form x−(shift). Since π/2÷3=π/6, it is a translation by π/6 in the positive x-direction. Putting in x=π/6 gives 3x−π/2=0, so sin0=0, which matches y=2sin3x being 0 at x=0.

n-m-h2-trig-02.title: What is the shortest interval at which sin²x repeats?
n-m-h2-trig-02.goal: Examine the claim "the period of sin x is 2π, so sin²x also has period 2π" by checking the repetition-interval equation, and state the smallest positive period with reasons.
n-m-h2-trig-02.material: Seoyeon said, "The period of sin x is 2π, so the period of y=sin²x is also 2π," and Minho said, "That is not the shortest interval." Here, the period means the smallest positive p for which f(x+p)=f(x) holds for all x. (sin²x is the square of sin x.)
n-m-h2-trig-02.thinking.0: Distinguishing a repeating interval from the smallest interval
n-m-h2-trig-02.thinking.2: Evaluating a claim by giving reasons
n-m-h2-trig-02.prereq.0: Periodic functions and the meaning of period
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the correct statements about f(x)=sin²x.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.hint.0: In each statement, put specific values such as 0 or π/2 in for x and compare whether the two sides are equal.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.hint.1: First write how sin(x+π) relates to sin x, then see what happens when you square.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.o.a: The period of sin x is 2π, so the shortest interval at which sin²x repeats must also be 2π
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.r.a: This treats the period of the original function as the shortest interval of the new function. Check that squaring removes the sign.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.o.b: For all x, sin²(x+π)=sin²x, so after moving by π the graph repeats in the same shape
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment made after writing how sin(x+π) relates to sin x and looking at the squared result.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.o.c: For all x, sin²(x+π/2)=sin²x, so after moving by π/2 the graph repeats in the same shape
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.r.c: You did not check by putting in specific values for x. For example, calculate both sides at x=0.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.o.d: For all x, sin²(x+2π)=sin²x, so after moving by 2π the graph repeats in the same shape
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.r.d: You did not miss that 2π is also a repeating interval. But whether it is the shortest must be examined separately.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s1.explain: sin(x+π)=−sin x, so sin²(x+π)=sin²x. So π is also a repeating interval, and so is 2π, twice π. But at x=0, sin²0=0, and sin²(π/2)=1, so π/2 is not a repeating interval. 2π is a repeating interval but not the shortest one.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.prompt: Write the smallest positive period of y=sin²x, and explain with reasons what is lacking in Seoyeon's statement. (Reasons: at least one of rewriting the expression or values of the graph)
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate the values of sin²x at x=0 and x=π/2, and find the interval over which the values become equal.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.hint.1: Recall whether you can rewrite sin²x as an expression containing cos2x.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.placeholder: Example: the smallest positive period of y=sin²x is ... because ...
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you rewrite the expression as sin²x=(1−cos2x)/2 or put in values of x directly?
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 2π is a repeating interval but not the shortest?
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you keep to the meaning of the word "smallest"?
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.model.0: sin²x=(1−cos2x)/2 and the period of cos2x is π, so the period of sin²x is π. Seoyeon's 2π also gives the same values after moving that far, but it is not the smallest interval.
n-m-h2-trig-02.s.s2.model.1: sin(x+π)=−sin x, so squaring gives sin²(x+π)=sin²x. So the minimal period is at most π, and the gap between x=π/2 and 3π/2, where sin²x is 1, is π, so π is the smallest. 2π is a repeating interval, but it is not the smallest.

n-m-h2-trig-03.title: If tan(α+β)=1, what is α+β?
n-m-h2-trig-03.goal: Follow how the judgment that a single tan value seems to determine the angle changes when information about the range of the angle arrives, and explain why.
n-m-h2-trig-03.material: For angles α and β, tanα=1/2 and tanβ=1/3. Information is revealed one piece at a time, so judge using only what is known so far. (tan(α+β) is (tanα+tanβ)÷(1−tanα·tanβ).)
n-m-h2-trig-03.thinking.0: Revising the judgment according to new information
n-m-h2-trig-03.thinking.1: Finding tan(α+β) with the addition formula
n-m-h2-trig-03.thinking.2: Using trigonometric values together with the range of the angle
n-m-h2-trig-03.prereq.1: The relation among angles with the same tan value (period π)
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment using only the information so far.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, first write the range in which α+β can lie.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many angles with tan value 1 are in that range.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the value of tan(α+β)?
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The numerator is 1/2+1/3=5/6 and the denominator is 1−1/6=5/6, so tan(α+β)=1.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This takes the sum of the tans to be the tan of the sum. Look again at how the denominator of the addition formula is written.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Check from the shape of the addition formula where the product is used.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You put the values straight into the formula and calculated numerator 5/6 and denominator 1−1/6=5/6.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.1.info: α and β are both acute angles (greater than 0° and less than 90°).
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The sum of two acute angles is greater than 0° and less than 180°. In this range, 45° is the only angle with tan value 1.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You used that the sum is between 0° and 180° and that within it there is exactly one angle with tan value 1.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You thought α+β could be greater than 180°. Work out the range of the sum of two acute angles.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It is true that there are several angles with the same tan value, but you did not use the given range.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The condition has changed. tanα=1/2 and tanβ=1/3 stay the same, α is an angle in the third quadrant (greater than 180° and less than 270°), and β is acute.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.2.after: α+β is greater than 180° and less than 360°. In this range, 225° is the only angle with tan 1. Even for the same tan value, the answer changes when the range of the angle changes.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You looked only at the tan value being 1 and reused the angle from before.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You seem to think that, because the range changed, it cannot be determined. Count how many angles in the new range have tan 1.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You found the angle with tan 1 in the new range 180°<α+β<360°.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s1.reflect: The value tan(α+β)=1 was the same, but depending on the information about the range of the angle it became 45° in one case and 225° in the other. The angle is not determined by the value of a trigonometric function alone; the range of the angle is also needed.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain why knowing tan(α+β)=1 does not determine α+β uniquely, and what the information about the range of the angle does.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.hint.0: Find and write an angle other than 45° whose tan value is 1.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the number of candidate angles without range information and with it.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: angles with the same tan value are ... If there is a range, ...
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you give an example of angles with the same tan value (45° and 225°)?
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say how the range narrows the candidates to one?
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.model.0: Angles with tan value 1 are not only 45° but repeat every 180°, like 225°, so the angle is not determined uniquely. If there is a range, such as acute or third quadrant, only one candidate remains within it.
n-m-h2-trig-03.s.s2.model.1: tan gives the same value at intervals of 180°, so from the value 1 alone you cannot tell whether it is 45° or 225°. You need to know which range the angle is in to pick one of the two.

n-m-h2-trig-04.title: Finding three side lengths that form an obtuse triangle
n-m-h2-trig-04.goal: Using the law of cosines, write the condition for the angle opposite the longest side to be obtuse, while also checking the condition for the triangle to actually exist, and build different obtuse triangles.
n-m-h2-trig-04.material: You want to make an obtuse triangle whose three side lengths are all natural numbers. Let c be the length of the longest side and a and b the other two sides, and use the law of cosines to examine the sign of cosC=(a²+b²−c²)÷(2ab), the cosine of the angle C opposite c.
n-m-h2-trig-04.thinking.0: Using the sign from the law of cosines to tell the kind of angle
n-m-h2-trig-04.thinking.1: Checking a hidden condition (existence of the triangle)
n-m-h2-trig-04.thinking.2: Building several examples that satisfy the conditions
n-m-h2-trig-04.prereq.1: The condition for a triangle to be formed from three side lengths
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.prompt: Minsu said, "If a=3, b=4, c=9, then c²=81 is greater than a²+b²=25, so cosC<0, and there is an obtuse triangle with sides 3, 4, 9." How do you judge this statement?
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine whether you could make a triangle from three sticks of length 3, 4, and 9.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.hint.1: Actually calculate the value of cosC and compare it with the range of values cosine can take.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.o.a: Correct. 9²>3²+4², so the angle opposite the longest side is obtuse
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the sign of the cosine value and did not check whether the triangle can actually be formed.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. 3+4<9, so a triangle cannot be formed with sides of these lengths
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.r.b: Before finding the cosine value, you first checked whether the three sides form a triangle.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.o.c: Wrong. If 9²>3²+4², the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.r.c: You mixed up the case of a right angle and the case of an obtuse angle. For 3, 4, 5, compare 5² with 3²+4².
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.o.d: Correct. 3, 4, 9 are different lengths, so it can be an obtuse triangle
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.r.d: The lengths being different has nothing to do with whether the triangle exists.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s1.explain: cosC=(9+16−81)÷24 equals −56÷24<−1, so it cannot be a cosine value. This is because 3+4<9, so no triangle is formed by the three sides. For an obtuse angle, the square of the longest side must be greater than the sum of the squares of the other two sides, and at the same time the longest side must be less than the sum of the other two.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different obtuse triangles whose side lengths are all natural numbers at most 20 and enter the three side lengths. (Triangles that differ only in order are regarded as the same triangle.)
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the longest side c first, then pick a and b in the range where a+b is greater than c.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.hint.1: For the three numbers you chose, calculate c² and a²+b² and compare them, and also compare a+b with c.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The three numbers are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The three numbers must be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two, so a triangle is formed.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The longest side is at least the sum of the other two, so no triangle is formed.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The square of the longest side is greater than the sum of the squares of the other two, so it is an obtuse triangle.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The square of the longest side is not greater than the sum of the squares of the other two, so it is not an obtuse triangle.
n-m-h2-trig-04.s.s2.explain: (3, 4, 6) has 6²=36>3²+4²=25 and 3+4>6. (4, 5, 8) has 64>41 and 9>8, and (5, 6, 10) has 100>61 and 11>10. (3, 4, 9) satisfies the square condition but 3+4<9, so it is not a triangle.

n-m-h2-trig-05.title: What do you need to know to find the radius of the circumscribed circle?
n-m-h2-trig-05.goal: Distinguish whether the triangle is determined uniquely from whether the value you want is determined uniquely, pick out the information that determines the radius of the circumscribed circle, and explain why.
n-m-h2-trig-05.material: In triangle ABC, a=BC, b=CA, c=AB, and A, B, C are the angles at the vertices. You want to know the radius R of the circumscribed circle. Each piece of information is given as specific numbers, and such a triangle is assumed to actually exist.
n-m-h2-trig-05.thinking.0: Picking out the information needed for the value you want
n-m-h2-trig-05.thinking.1: Using the law of sines a/sinA=2R
n-m-h2-trig-05.thinking.2: Seeing that the value can be the same even with two triangles
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all of the following cases in which that information alone determines the value of R uniquely.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.hint.0: In the law of sines a/sinA=b/sinB=c/sinC=2R, write what expression you get if there is at least one pair of a side and its opposite angle.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each piece of information, check whether there is a pair of a side and its corresponding angle, and if not, whether one can be made with the law of cosines.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.o.a: The sizes of the three angles A, B, C
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.r.a: Think about the fact that three angles alone give infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.o.b: The length of one side a and the size of its opposite angle A
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.r.b: This judgment holds that a single pair from the law of sines (a side and its opposite angle) is enough to find R.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.o.c: The lengths of two sides a, b and the size of angle A
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.r.c: Even with information that allows two triangles, you checked separately whether R is determined. See whether this information contains a pair of a side and its opposite angle.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.o.d: The length of one side a and the size of one adjacent angle B
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.r.d: Think about the fact that the remaining angle C can be changed freely, so R changes too.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.o.e: The lengths of two sides a, b and the size of the included angle C
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.r.e: You used the fact that finding the third side with the law of cosines creates a pair of a side and its opposite angle.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s1.explain: For b, R comes straight from a/sinA=2R. c is the same as b, because a and A are a corresponding pair. Even if two triangles can be formed, a/sinA is the same, so R is a single value. For e, find c with the law of cosines and then use c/sinC=2R. For a, knowing only the three angles gives many similar triangles of different sizes, so R is not determined, and for d, R changes when C changes.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.prompt: The option "a, b and angle A" is information that can give two triangles, yet R is determined uniquely. Explain why.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write the law of sines and count which letters are involved in finding R.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.hint.1: Assuming two triangles, compare whether a and A are the same or different.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.placeholder: Example: in the law of sines, ...
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the expression that solves a/sinA=2R for R?
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that b is not used to find R?
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that a and A are the same even with two triangles?
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.model.0: From the law of sines a/sinA=2R, R=a/(2sinA). This uses only a and A and not b, so even if two triangles are formed, a and A are the same and so R is the same.
n-m-h2-trig-05.s.s2.model.1: If you have a side a and its opposite angle A, the law of sines immediately gives 2R=a/sinA. Even if the third side or the other angles differ between the two triangles, this value is the same, so R is determined uniquely.

n-m-h2-trig-06.title: Making a triangle with integer sides and one angle of 60°
n-m-h2-trig-06.goal: Use cos60°=1/2 in the law of cosines to set up the relation among the sides of a triangle with a 60° angle, and build non-similar triangles whose side lengths are all integers.
n-m-h2-trig-06.material: In triangle ABC, a=BC, b=CA, c=AB and ∠C=60°. You want to build a triangle whose three side lengths are all natural numbers.
n-m-h2-trig-06.thinking.0: Setting up the relation from the law of cosines
n-m-h2-trig-06.thinking.1: Building an example that satisfies the conditions yourself
n-m-h2-trig-06.thinking.2: Filtering out trivial and similar examples
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct relation among a, b, c when ∠C=60°.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.hint.0: First write the law of cosines as it is, then put in the value of cos60°.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.hint.1: Put a=b=c=1 (an equilateral triangle) into each equation to test which one is correct.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.r.a: In −2ab cosC of the law of cosines, you took cos60° to be 1. Check the value of cos60° again.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.r.b: The sign was written the opposite way. Think about what angle gives this sign.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.r.c: You put cos60°=1/2 into −2ab cosC and calculated.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.r.d: You wrote the relation for a right triangle. Check whether ∠C is a right angle.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s1.explain: The law of cosines is c²=a²+b²−2ab cosC and cos60°=1/2, so c²=a²+b²−ab. If the sign were +ab, then ∠C=120°, and if c²=a²+b², then ∠C=90°.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 non-similar triangles with ∠C=60° and all three sides natural numbers (at most 40), and enter a, b, c. (Exclude the equilateral triangle, a and b must have no common divisor other than 1, and triangles that differ only by swapping a and b are regarded as the same triangle.)
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one a and change b to 1, 2, 3, ... while calculating a²+b²−ab.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the result is the square of some natural number.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The three numbers are natural numbers at most 40.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The three numbers must be natural numbers from 1 to 40.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.fail.c2: c² is not equal to a²+b²−ab, so ∠C is not 60°.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.ok.c3: It is not an equilateral triangle.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.fail.c3: If a=b, the triangle is equilateral. Equilateral triangles are excluded.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.ok.c4: The only common divisor of a and b is 1.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.fail.c4: a and b have a common divisor greater than 1, so this is a similar triangle scaled up from a smaller one.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Write in one or two sentences how you found that triangle.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Fix one value of a, then think about what value you computed as you changed b.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Say what number that value would have to be in order to be c².
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compute while changing a and b?
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether the computed value is a perfect square?
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.model.0: I fixed a=3 and computed a²+b²−ab while changing b. When b=8, it was 49, a square number. So c=7.
n-m-h2-trig-06.s.s2.because.model.1: I plugged a and b in turn into the relation c²=a²+b²−ab and looked for cases where the result is a perfect square.

n-m-h2-trig-07.title: Helping Harin with the sin75° solution
n-m-h2-trig-07.goal: Find the first wrong line in a friend's solution that misuses the addition formula, pick the clue that shows the result is impossible, and write a message that lets your friend fix it on their own.
n-m-h2-trig-07.material: Harin tried to find sin75° by writing 75°=45°+30° and solved it as shown below. (√2 means the square root of 2.) Harin is your friend.
n-m-h2-trig-07.thinking.0: Find the first wrong line in the solution
n-m-h2-trig-07.thinking.1: Notice the error from the range of the result
n-m-h2-trig-07.thinking.2: Write a note to send to your friend
n-m-h2-trig-07.prereq.0: Addition formulas for sine and cosine
n-m-h2-trig-07.prereq.1: The values of sin45°, sin30°, cos45°, cos30°
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Harin's solution that is wrong.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line in order and check whether it really follows from the previous line.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s1.hint.1: Test each line's formula one by one by plugging in easy angles such as A=B=30°.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s1.line.0: Since 75°=45°+30°, we use the addition formula.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. The addition formula for sine is sin(A+B)=sinA cosB+cosA sinB. Lines 3 and 4 are calculations that follow the wrong formula, and the values of sin45° and sin30° themselves are correct.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.prompt: Even if you do not know the correct addition formula, what clue immediately tells you that Harin's result is wrong?
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.hint.0: First recall the range of values that sin can take.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate Harin's value as a decimal and compare it with that range.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.o.a: 75° is an acute angle, so sin75° must be less than sin30°=1/2
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.r.a: This assumes that sine only decreases on acute angles. Compare the sine values of 30° and 75°.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.o.b: A sine value cannot exceed 1, but the result (√2+1)/2 is greater than 1
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.r.b: You compared the computed result with the range of sine values, from −1 to 1 inclusive.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.o.c: √2/2+1/2 is irrational, so it cannot be the value of sin75°
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.r.c: This assumes that a value cannot be a sine value just because it is irrational. sin45°=√2/2 is also irrational.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.o.d: The sine of 45° and the sine of 30° cannot be added to each other
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.r.d: This assumes that adding them is itself forbidden. There is no reason they cannot be added. You have to judge by the result.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s2.explain: (√2+1)/2 is about 1.207, which is greater than 1. A sine value is between −1 and 1 inclusive, so the calculation must be wrong somewhere. Even without knowing the formula, you can notice the error from the range of values alone. The correct formula is sin75°=sin45°cos30°+cos45°sin30°.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Harin. Include ① which part of the solution is the problem and ② one way Harin can check it on their own, but ③ do not write the finished value of sin75°.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.hint.0: Start by finding one thing Harin did correctly and acknowledging it.
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.hint.1: Then write one action Harin can try directly (checking the range of values, plugging in an easy angle, etc.).
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you acknowledge what Harin did correctly (splitting into 45° and 30°)?
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the action Harin should try clear?
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid giving the finished value away?
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.model.0: Splitting it into 45°+30° was a good idea. But the addition formula on line 2 is the problem. You got about 1.2, but a sine value cannot exceed 1, so check that. Why not also test whether that formula is right by plugging in values like A=B=30°?
n-m-h2-trig-07.s.s3.model.1: You were right to split 75° into 45° and 30°. But the formula saying sin(A+B) equals sinA+sinB looks odd. The result should not be greater than 1, so please check the addition formula for sine again in your textbook.

n-m-h2-trig-08.title: Height of a tower seen from two points
n-m-h2-trig-08.goal: Understand that having an angle and a distance does not mean there is only one value: work out the two possible arrangements by calculation, then rewrite the problem with a condition that fixes just one.
n-m-h2-trig-08.material: A tower stands on flat ground. The base of the tower P and the points A and B lie on one line, and AB=20 m. The angle of elevation to the top of the tower is 30° from A and 45° from B. Ignore eye height. Seoyun said, "We have both the angles and the distance, so the height of the tower is determined uniquely," and Hajun said, "It could be thought of differently."
n-m-h2-trig-08.thinking.0: Judge how many answers the given information determines
n-m-h2-trig-08.thinking.2: Fix the problem by adding a condition
n-m-h2-trig-08.prereq.1: The relationship between height and distance in a right triangle
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct judgment about whose statement is right.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.hint.0: Draw all the possible arrangements when A, B, and P are on one line.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.hint.1: In each arrangement, check whether you can express the distances from P to A and from P to B in terms of the height h.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.o.a: Seoyun: There are two angles of elevation and a distance, so the height is definitely determined uniquely
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.r.a: Even if there seems to be a lot of information, you must separately check whether the figure is determined uniquely.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.o.b: Hajun: We do not know the distance to the base of the tower, so the height is not determined in any case
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.r.b: This overstates that it is not determined. Calculate whether the angles let you reduce it to a single distance.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.o.c: Hajun: The height differs depending on whether the two points are on the same side or opposite sides of the base of the tower
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that the given statement does not fix the arrangement uniquely.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.o.d: Seoyun: The two angles of elevation are different, so A and B are definitely on opposite sides of the base of the tower
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.r.d: You concluded the positions from the fact that the angles differ. Think about whether, even on the same side, the nearer point sees the top at a larger angle.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s1.explain: If they are on the same side, the angle of elevation from the nearer point B (45°) is larger, and even if they are on opposite sides, the angles can be given as 30° and 45°. Two figures are possible and the heights differ too (calculated in the next step), so the problem must specify one arrangement. That does not mean the calculation is impossible. Once the arrangement is fixed, the height is determined.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.prompt: Let the height be h. Find ① the height h1 when A and B are on the same side of the base P, and ② the height h2 when P is between A and B (opposite sides), and enter each to two decimal places. (in m)
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the height as h and express PA and PB in terms of h using right triangles.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.hint.1: Use the fact that the difference of the two distances is 20 when they are on the same side, and the sum is 20 when they are on opposite sides.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.var.h1: Height h1 when on the same side
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.var.h2: Height h2 when on opposite sides
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.ok.c2: On the same side, it satisfies √3·h−h=20.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.fail.c2: On the same side, PA−PB=20. Set up the equation with PA=√3·h and PB=h.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.fail.c3: On opposite sides, PA+PB=20. Set up the equation with PA=√3·h and PB=h.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s2.explain: If the angle from A is 30°, PA=h÷tan30°=√3·h, and if the angle from B is 45°, PB=h. On the same side, PA−PB=20, so h=20÷(√3−1)=10(√3+1)≈27.32. On opposite sides, PA+PB=20, so h=20÷(√3+1)=10(√3−1)≈7.32.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite this problem by adding just one sentence so that the height is determined uniquely.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.hint.0: Recall again how many possible arrangements there were.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write one sentence that chooses one of them.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you read the added sentence to check that it fixes the arrangement uniquely?
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the positional relationship of A, B, and P?
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.model.0: Add one sentence saying that A and B are on the same side of the base P of the tower.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.model.1: The base of the tower P is between A and B.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.model.2: The base of the tower P is on segment AB.
n-m-h2-trig-08.s.s3.model.3: We are told that the distance from A to the base of the tower P is 20√3 m.

n-m-h2-trig-09.title: Checking a maximum-value solution on a given interval
n-m-h2-trig-09.goal: Find that a solution using the combination of trigonometric functions to get a maximum never used the range of x, then check the endpoints of the interval to find the correct maximum.
n-m-h2-trig-09.material: Hyunwoo found the maximum of y=3sinx+4cosx for 0≤x≤π/6 as shown below. (Angles are in radians. α is the acute angle with cosα=3/5 and sinα=4/5, and α is about 0.93.)
n-m-h2-trig-09.thinking.0: Find the first wrong line in the solution
n-m-h2-trig-09.thinking.1: Check whether that maximum actually occurs within the interval
n-m-h2-trig-09.thinking.2: Calculate the values at the endpoints of the interval
n-m-h2-trig-09.prereq.1: Increasing and decreasing behavior of the sine function
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Hyunwoo's solution that is wrong.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.hint.0: Check in the sentence under what condition the maximum on line 2 came from.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.hint.1: For the maximum to be 5, you need an x for which sin(x+α) is 1. Consider whether that x lies in the interval of the problem.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.line.1: If x is any real number, the maximum of sin(x+α) is 1, so the maximum of y is 5.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.line.2: Therefore the maximum on 0≤x≤π/6 is also 5.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.line.3: This is because sin(x+α)=1 can happen within the interval as well.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The 5 on line 2 is the maximum when x is any real number. For sin(x+α)=1, we need x=π/2−α (about 0.64), which is greater than π/6 (about 0.52), so it is outside the interval. Line 4 is the wrong reason for line 3.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.prompt: Find the maximum of y on 0≤x≤π/6, and also write why Hyunwoo's 5 cannot occur on this interval.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.hint.0: Find the x for which sin(x+α)=1 and compare it with the interval of the problem.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.hint.1: See how x+α changes over the interval (whether it increases or decreases) and decide where the maximum occurs.
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The x for which sin(x+α)=1 is ... so the maximum is ...
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the x that gives the maximum is in the interval?
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the value at the endpoint of the interval directly?
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say how x+α changes over the interval?
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.model.0: The x with sin(x+α)=1 is π/2−α (about 0.64), which is greater than π/6 (about 0.52), so it is outside the interval. On the interval y increases, so the maximum is at x=π/6, and it is 3·1/2+4·√3/2=3/2+2√3 (about 4.96).
n-m-h2-trig-09.s.s2.model.1: x+α moves from α (about 0.93) to π/6+α (about 1.45), staying at most π/2, so it keeps increasing. So the maximum is at the endpoint x=π/6, where y=(3+4√3)/2≈4.96. To get 5, x would have to be outside the interval, so 5 is not possible.

n-m-h2-trig-10.title: Angle sizes and trigonometric ratio sizes in a triangle
n-m-h2-trig-10.goal: Under the condition that A, B, C are interior angles of a triangle, judge in which direction comparing angle sizes carries over to comparing sin, cos, tan values, and give reasons using the law of sines and obtuse angles.
n-m-h2-trig-10.material: Four students made the following claims about the three interior angles A, B, C of triangle ABC. Consider only cases where the trigonometric ratio values are defined.
n-m-h2-trig-10.thinking.0: Judge whether a statement is true or false within its conditions
n-m-h2-trig-10.thinking.1: Connect angles and sides with the law of sines
n-m-h2-trig-10.prereq.1: The property that the side opposite the larger angle is the longer side
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the claims that are always correct in triangle ABC.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.hint.0: Plug specific angles (30°, 100°, etc.) in for A and B in each claim.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.hint.1: Use the law of sines to convert sinA and sinB into side lengths, and write how the size comparison turns out.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.r.a: This judges that a larger angle has a larger sine value. You can check it by comparing the lengths of the sides opposite the two angles using the law of sines.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.r.b: This judges that a larger cosine means a larger angle. See how the cosine value changes as the angle increases from 0° to 180°.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.r.c: You converted the size of the sine values into side lengths to compare them and used the fact that the larger side lies opposite the larger angle.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.r.d: You overlooked that an angle of a triangle can be obtuse. Compare the two tan values when A=30° and B=100°.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s1.explain: By the law of sines, a=2R·sinA and b=2R·sinB, so sinA>sinB is equivalent to a>b, and since the larger side is opposite the larger angle, it is also equivalent to A>B. So a and c are both correct. If cosA>cosB, then A<B, so b is backwards, and tan is negative for an obtuse angle, so when A=30° and B=100°, tanA>tanB but A<B, which makes d false.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.prompt: Explain why "if sinA>sinB, then A>B" holds in a triangle (c), and give one counterexample showing that (d) does not hold.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.hint.0: Rewrite sinA and sinB as side lengths using the law of sines.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.hint.1: Take one of A and B to be obtuse and consider the sign of the tan value.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. By the law of sines ... Counterexample: A=..., B=...
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you turn the comparison of sine values into a comparison of side lengths?
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you actually compare the values of tan A and tan B?
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you show in your counterexample that A<B but tanA>tanB?
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.model.0: By the law of sines, a=2R sinA and b=2R sinB, so if sinA>sinB then a>b. The larger side is opposite the larger angle, so A>B. Counterexample: A=30°, B=100°. tan30° is positive and tan100° is negative, so tanA>tanB but A<B.
n-m-h2-trig-10.s.s2.model.1: If sinA>sinB, then by the law of sines side a is longer than side b, and then A is larger than B. tan is negative for an obtuse angle, so for example if A=45° and B=120°, then tanA=1>tanB=−√3 but A<B.
